activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first instant replay on television was shown by CBS during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963, using a system devised by director Tony Verna.
story:
The living room smelled of chili and wet coats, and by the third quarter every seat was taken except the piano bench, which nobody wanted because it faced away from the television. Daniel sat on the arm of the couch with his phone flat on his knee. His father and uncle occupied the couch like opposing generals, while Tyler and Nikola had claimed the floor between the coffee table and the screen. On the far chair, their neighbor Ms. Whitehead knitted something long and gray and watched the game with an attention that suggested she understood more of it than she admitted.

The play happened fast, the way disputed plays always do. The receiver stretched for the sideline, the ball came loose as he hit the ground, and the referee's arms went up in a way nobody could read from across the room. The uncle roared that it was a catch. Daniel's father roared that it was a fumble. Tyler was on his feet demanding the network show it again, as if volume could summon the footage, and Nikola leaned toward the screen with her hands pressed flat on the carpet.

"That was a catch. They have to show it again. They always show it again."

"They don't have to," Daniel said, though he wanted the replay too, maybe more than anyone, because the receiver was his team's receiver and the doubt was unbearable. "The broadcast can show whatever the director wants. It's not a rule, it's a choice."

Ms. Whitehead looked up from her knitting. "A choice," she said. "That's an interesting word for it."

The network cut to a punt return, then to a commercial, then to two men at a desk talking about the weather in a city none of them had ever visited. Tyler threw a piece of popcorn at the screen. Daniel's uncle declared the whole broadcast corrupt. Nikola, who had gone quiet in the way she did when she was thinking, said, "But they can do it, right? Rewind it live? Somebody figured out how to do that the first time."

Daniel looked at his phone. He had meant to check the score, but instead he typed a question into the search bar, partly to end the argument and partly because the argument had opened a door in him he hadn't known was there: the question of whether seeing it again would even settle anything, or whether people just dichotomize into those who trust the first look and those who demand the second. The result came up in small gray text, and he read it twice before saying it out loud.

"The first instant replay on television was CBS, during the Army-Navy game, December 7, 1963. The system was devised by a director named Tony Verna." He said it carefully, the way he'd learned to read aloud in class, and the room went half quiet. "So it's not ancient. It's not like the game itself. Somebody had to invent it."

Tyler, from where he now sat on the floor, arms crossed, watched Daniel's face rather than the phone. The kid had done it again, pulled some fact out of the air like a card from a sleeve, and made everyone else feel like they'd been watching the world with one eye closed. Sixty-some years ago a director had built a machine so that people in living rooms could stop arguing, except the arguing never stopped, Tyler knew that from his own house, where his mother replayed every family grievance on a loop nobody had invented for her. He wanted the catch to be real. He wanted it so badly his jaw ached.

"They're going back to it," Nikola said.

They were. The broadcast returned from commercial and, almost casually, showed the play again, slowed, from the one angle that made everything obvious. The ball had come out before the receiver's knee touched. It was a fumble. Ms. Whitehead set down her needles. Daniel's father stood up with both hands raised, vindicated, while the uncle stared at the screen as though it had personally deceived him, which in a sense it had, because the replay had been on his side right up until it existed.

Tyler turned around from the floor and looked up at Daniel, and his voice came out lighter than he felt. "Next time don't tell us anything. We were happier before you invented the replay."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Caramelization is the browning of sugar on its own, without proteins; table sugar begins to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius.
story:
The community kitchen on Alder Street smelled like burnt toast and hope, mostly the first one, and David had claimed the back burner because it was the only one that behaved. He was making dinner for his family, which sounded noble until you knew the family would be eating it at a folding table beside strangers, because their oven had died on Tuesday and Ms. Sok had said, in her flat, noncommittal way, "Saturday night, six o'clock, don't be late." So here he was on Saturday at four, with sugar, cream, a dented saucepan, and a plan that did not entirely deserve the word.

The dinner part was fine. He could do rice, he could do the chicken his mother had taught him before she started working nights, and the flatbread was Reem's job anyway. The problem was dessert. He had promised Anabel something with caramel, back when promising things had felt free, and caramel was a substance he did not trust. Sugar in a pan, nothing else, waiting for it to turn. His father called recipes like this the family patrimony, which was a fancy word for a fat folder of stained index cards, half of them in a script David couldn't read, and not one of them mentioned temperatures. "Cook until it smells right," the card said, which was the kind of advice that sounded wise right up until the smoke alarm went off.

"Caramelization," Reem said, reading over his shoulder from a page on his phone, one eyebrow up like the word had personally offended him. "That's what it's called, the browning of sugar on its own, no proteins, nothing else in the pan. Table sugar starts to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius."

"That's hot," David said.

"That's specific," Reem said. "Unlike you."

"I'm specific. I'm specifically winging it."

Anabel arrived then with the cream and a candy thermometer she had taken from her grandmother's drawer without asking, which she announced proudly, as though the theft augured well for the whole evening. She clipped it to the pan, and the three of them stood in a row watching sugar melt like it was television. David had the spoon in his hand and an argument in his head. His father's school said take it off when it smells right, when the color turns the color of old pennies, which was a way of thinking with your whole body, history in your nose. Reem's school said numbers, 170, trust the glass. Two ways of knowing, and only one pan of sugar.

"Taking it off early is safe," Anabel said. "Taking it off late is interesting."

"That's the worst slogan I've ever heard," David said, but he repeated it under his breath twice.

The sugar went glassy, then loose, then began, all at once, to color. Amber, then deeper, and David leaned in and breathed and thought, this is the smell, this is exactly the smell on the card, the one his father must have smelled in his father's kitchen, some chain of noses going back who knew how far. The thermometer read 168. One degree, maybe two, from where the science said the true change began. His hand was already moving.

He pulled it off the heat.

"You didn't wait," Reem said.

"It changed color before the number," David said. "Or it's changing right now because I got lucky. I genuinely can't tell you which."

"That's a terrible answer."

"It's an honest one. The nose and the number mostly agree, and when they don't, you pick, and then you live with your dessert."

He added the cream off the heat, carefully, because it hissed like a small angry animal, and the sauce came together glossy and dark and smelling of every kitchen in the folder at once. Anabel dipped a spoon and made a sound that was not quite a word. Reem, who had been proven approximately nothing, since the color and the temperature had arrived nearly together, took a taste anyway and gave a grudging nod, as if conceding a point in a debate he still thought he'd won on paper.

At six, the folding tables filled up. His parents came, his little sister came, and his father tasted the caramel on the flatbread and closed his eyes, and David waited for a verdict about tradition, about whether the thermometer was cheating. Instead his father said, "Where's mine to take home?" which was, David decided, the patrimony's way of saying thank you.

Then Ms. Sok appeared at his elbow with an empty jar and the folder under her arm, the folder, which she must have asked his mother to bring. "There's a card in here," she said, "in the front, the one in your grandmother's handwriting. You should look at the back of it."

He wiped his hands and opened the folder while Reem and Anabel crowded in, and there, on the back of the caramel card, in that same unreadable script, was one line in careful English: begins at 170 degrees, watch it close. His grandmother had known the number all along.

"Unbelievable," Reem said.

David laughed, dipped a spoon in the pot, and held it out. "Taste that. Nose and number, same pan, all along."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: One mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere of pressure.
story:
Kaylee dragged the cardboard boxes out of Mr. Levy's garage in a row, three of them, and stood looking at the space where his car had been. He had said she could use it while he was at work, as long as she swept up after, and she had said yes too quickly, before she understood what she actually wanted to do there. The retest was Friday. Fifty grams of calcium carbonate, heated, and she was supposed to say how many moles of carbon dioxide came off. She could do the arithmetic. What she could not do was believe it, and she had decided, standing in the kitchen at eleven the night before, that believing it was the whole problem.

Her father called it an amalgam of stubbornness and nerves, the thing that made her freeze on tests, though he said it kindly, over the dishes. Her mother offered to propitiate the chemistry teacher with an email, which Kaylee refused, because the teacher was not the problem and emails from mothers never helped anyone believe anything.

She took the measuring tape and marked a rectangle on the concrete with chalk. Her plan had come from Anjali, in a message she still had on her phone, sent from the hospital where Anjali's grandmother was being kept for observation. Anjali had written it during study hall, bored and worried, and Kaylee read it again now, leaning against the garage door.

"Okay so you always get the numbers right and then you write them down like they're a guess," the message said. "You wrote 'about 2 point whatever' on the quiz like you were sorry for having an opinion. Here's the thing my cousin told me. One mole of a gas, if it was ideal, at 0 degrees Celsius, at 1 atmosphere of pressure, would take up about 22.4 litres. She said to picture it. She actually measured a box. Do the box thing, Kay. Make it real and then you'll trust it. Also my grandmother says hi, she's fine, she's just mad they won't let her watch her shows."

The first box was too small; she had measured 22.4 centimetres on a side instead of litres of volume, and she stood inside its chalk outline feeling the error in her whole body, the smallness of it, before she recalculated. Twenty-two point four litres was not a cube at all in her head until she worked it out on paper on the hood of the lawnmower: about 28 centimetres on each side. She built the box out of the flattest cardboard and tape, and it was so ordinary it embarrassed her. It would sit on a shelf. A mole of carbon dioxide, all of it, would fit in a box she could carry under one arm.

Then the arithmetic. Fifty grams of calcium carbonate, divided by its molar mass, a hundred point something; then the equation said one mole of carbonate gave one mole of gas. Half a mole, nearly. She put her chalk numbers beside the box and looked between them, and the looking was the thing, the two ways of seeing stacked on each other. On the paper it was grams becoming moles, unit over unit, cancellation she could do in her sleep. On the floor it was half a box of gas, weightless, invisible, real enough that if she cut the tape the whole driveway would smell of nothing at all and the chalk numbers would still be true.

She thought about the first test, the one she had failed, and how she had written the answer and then crossed it out. Mr. Levy had found her at his mailbox that evening and asked, not in a teacherly way, since he was retired and taught nothing anymore, what the crossing out was for. She had said she didn't know if she was right, and he had said the bellicose thing, the thing she was still turning over: "The numbers aren't going to fight you. You're the only one in this fight." It had sounded harsh at the time. Now it sounded more like he had been describing the box. The gas didn't argue. It just took up the space it took up.

Anjali came after school, the day her grandmother was released, and stood in the garage doorway with her bike helmet still on. "That's it? That's the whole mole?"

"At zero degrees," Kaylee said. "At one atmosphere. If it's ideal."

Anjali came in and knocked on the cardboard with one knuckle, twice, like checking whether someone was home.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Payment history is the largest factor in a FICO credit score, making up about 35 percent of it for the general population.
story:
The line at the branch on Marsh Street was four deep when Lauren got there, and Shaelyn was already at the counter arguing with a man in a gray vest about the difference between what she'd been told and what the paperwork said. Lauren held the folded envelope with her name on it, the one from the phone company, the one with the red strip across the top, and watched her friend lean in.

"He said the payment cleared," Shaelyn said. "He said it four weeks ago."

"Payments post at the end of the cycle," the man said. He had the patient, choleric flush of someone who had explained this same thing since nine that morning and was one customer away from losing his composure entirely. "It posted late."

Lauren stepped up beside Shaelyn and set her envelope on the counter. Inside was a bill for sixty-eight dollars, marked past due, with a smaller number below it labeled interest. Not much. A dollar and change. Still, it had grown from nothing in six weeks, the way a drip fills a bucket if you leave the room long enough.

"I forgot this one," she said. "Does that go somewhere? Like, does it count against me?"

The man turned to his screen. "Are you asking about your credit score?"

"I'm asking if one missed phone bill follows me around."

"Payment history is the biggest piece of a FICO score," he said, typing. "About thirty-five percent of it, for the general population." He said it the way a bus driver announces stops, flat, no emphasis, a fact he carried like loose change.

Shaelyn turned around. "Thirty-five percent? For one bill?"

"The piece is thirty-five percent," Lauren said slowly, working it through. "Not the bill. The bill's a fraction of the piece." She looked at the envelope. "So it's a fraction of a fraction, but it's the heaviest fraction there is." The man gave a small shrug that conceded nothing and confirmed everything.

He slid a brochure across the counter. On the front, two curving lines, one climbing, one sinking, and beneath them the words compound interest. "You're eighteen? Open a savings account while you're here. Same force that charged you a dollar forty works the other way if the bank owes you."

"The bank owes me?"

"If you deposit." He almost smiled. "It's not generosity. It's arithmetic."

Lauren sat in the chair beside his desk while he opened the account, and Shaelyn hovered, reading every screen upside down like a customs inspector. The interest rate on savings was small, smaller than the penalty rate on her late bill, and Lauren said so.

"That's because you're the borrower in one case and the lender in the other," the man said. "You charge less when you're the safe bet." He tapped the loan disclosure form on his desk. "This one amortizes. Car loan. The payments get applied a little differently each month, interest first, principal later, until it's gone."

"Amortize," Shaelyn repeated. "That sounds like something a pedagogue would say before confiscating your phone."

"It means the loan gets paid off in pieces," Lauren said, and was surprised to find she knew it, some fragment from her mother's refinance papers spread across the kitchen table last spring, her mother's finger moving down the column while her father stood at the window not looking at any of it.

The man set two forms in front of her. One would put two hundred dollars, her entire graduation money, into savings, where it would grow slowly and invisibly, a plant in a dark closet. The other was a secured card application, a line of credit she could build by buying gas and paying it off, on time, every time, which was the whole trick, and which was the thing she had just proven she couldn't reliably do with a phone bill.

"I can do both," she said.

"You can," the man said. "Most people don't."

"Most people think one late bill means game over," Shaelyn said. "Or they think it means nothing."

"Both wrong," the man said.

Lauren signed the savings form first, then took the card application and held it, pen over the line. She thought about how the same rule, the same thirty-five percent, would either save her or sink her depending on nothing but whether she remembered, in some month she couldn't yet picture, on some Tuesday that didn't exist yet, to pay sixty-eight dollars. She couldn't promise that. She signed anyway, because not signing promised nothing too, and nothing was smaller.

"Approved in seven to ten days," the man said, gathering the papers. "Congratulations, or condolences."

"Which one?"

He stacked her copies and slid them across. "Check back in a year and tell me."

Shaelyn picked up the envelope with the red strip. "Sixty-eight dollars," she said. "I'm setting a reminder on your phone right now."

"You're setting it on yours too," Lauren said. "Your bill posted late."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: An equilibrium is dynamic: the forward and reverse reactions keep happening, but at equal rates, so the amounts of reactants and products stay constant.
story:
Hannah got it right away, or at least that was what she told Preston, and she kept telling him until it sounded true to her too. Fourth period, Ms. Mendoza's room smelled like somebody's burnt popcorn and the radiators clanked under the windows, and on the board the word equilibrium sat in green marker with a double arrow beneath it, pointing both ways. Ms. Mendoza said only that the quiz on Tuesday would cover temperature effects, and that the class had thirty seconds of silence to look at the diagram before anyone spoke. Hannah spent those thirty seconds deciding she would rather be the kind of person who understood things quickly than the kind who asked, and so when Preston leaned over and whispered that the whole thing made his eyes cross, she said, "It's easy. It's just balance." She had not yet learned that saying a thing is balance is not the same as knowing how it behaves.

The trouble surfaced at lunch. Koralie had saved them a table near the vending machines, and Preston, unwrapping a sandwich, began describing the shop where his uncle worked, the one on Delmore Street that sold phone cases and incense. "It's weird," he said. "All afternoon people are coming in and going out, but the count stays the same. Like twenty people in the shop, always twenty, hour after hour." He tore the crust off his bread. "My uncle says it's the strangest thing, he can't explain it. It's like everything's moving and nothing's changing." Hannah said, "That's just a slow afternoon," and Koralie laughed, and the conversation moved to the winter dance, which was the zeitgeist of the entire school that week, every hallway conversation bending toward it whether you wanted it to or not. Hannah laughed too. But the shop had stuck in her somewhere, like a burr on a sweater, and she found herself drawing the double arrow on her napkin in ketchup.

Tuesday came, and the quiz, and Hannah got the temperature question wrong. The question asked what happens to a reaction at equilibrium when you heat it, and she had written that heating speeds everything up and the amounts stay the same, because if it was balance, and you pushed both sides equally, balance was what you got. Ms. Mendoza handed the quizzes back on Thursday without a lecture, which was her way. She wrote one comment in red at the bottom of Hannah's page: it moves, but not the way you think. Reread the handout. Ask the shop. Hannah read it three times. Ms. Mendoza had not been at lunch. Hannah did not know how her teacher knew about the shop, unless Preston had said something, and Preston would absolutely have said something, and she was going to kill him, in a friendly way, possibly.

She found Preston at his locker before fifth period, lugubrious as always in his gray hoodie, slumped like the locker itself was a disappointment to him. "You told Ms. Mendoza about your uncle's shop," she said. "Maybe," he said. "I tell her stuff. She listens. It's her whole thing." "So explain the shop to me," Hannah said, "because I got the quiz wrong and it's your fault, sort of, not really, but tell me anyway." Preston shut his locker. "Okay, so. People keep arriving, and people keep leaving, and the shop never empties and never fills. All afternoon, the same number of people are inside." "So nothing's happening." "Everything's happening," Preston said. "Arrivals, departures, both going the whole time. That's the point. The count stays constant because they're happening at the same rate." He looked at the ceiling as if checking his own accuracy. "The same rate," he repeated, slower, like the phrase was a coin he was turning over.

Hannah stood very still in the crowded hallway, transfixed, honestly, by how wrong she had been and how cleanly the wrongness could be replaced. It was not that nothing moved. It was that everything moved, forward and reverse, and the movement canceled itself out in the counting, and the counting was what stayed constant. The forward reaction and the reverse reaction were both happening, both going, and because they went at equal rates, the amounts of what you started with and what you ended up with just sat there, fixed, while underneath them the traffic never stopped. "So when you heat it," she said slowly, "you're changing one of the rates. Or both, but not the same. So the count changes until..." She stopped. She did not actually know the until-what, and she was surprised to find she could say so out loud, in a hallway, in front of Preston. "I still don't get the temperature part. I just get that it isn't frozen."

That night Koralie sent her a message, and Hannah read it sitting cross-legged on her bed with the handout open beside her and a pencil she was not using. "you looked wrecked after the quiz," Koralie wrote, "and then you acted fine at lunch which, no offense, was maybe the least convincing performance of the year. also preston told me about the shop thing. i think you're mad at yourself for pretending you understood it in the first place. which, fair. but also you're the only one keeping score." Hannah typed three replies and deleted them. The first was defensive. The second was a joke. The third said, you're right, and she deleted that one too, because she was not sure it was entirely true, and she was trying, this week at least, not to say things she had not checked.

She wrote back, "quiz corrections due monday. come to the library saturday, bring the handout, i'll bring my wrong answer and we can be wrong in new ways together." Koralie replied with a single thumbs-up, which Hannah understood to mean yes and also I'm still keeping an eye on you.

Saturday, in the library's back corner where the radiators ticked, Hannah laid out her old quiz and wrote her correction: heating shifts the reaction, one way or the other, and the amounts change, and what stays is not the stillness but the equal-and-opposite motion underneath, forward and reverse still both happening, still going, rates equal again once it settles at a new constant. Ms. Mendoza had not explained any of it, and Preston had not really either, and Hannah could not have said which piece came from the handout and which came from a phone-case shop on Delmore Street, or whether the shop metaphor would survive the next quiz intact. She put a question mark next to the word settles and left it there. Koralie leaned over, read the page, and tapped the question mark with one finger. "You're keeping that?" "I'm keeping it," Hannah said, and pulled the pencil back out.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Stage directions in a script are usually set apart in italics or parentheses so actors and directors can tell them from spoken lines.
story:
The debate tournament ran until six, but Michael's packet for the young playwrights' showcase said scripts were due at seven the same evening, and so he sat in the empty cafeteria of the host school with a legal pad and a borrowed laptop that held a dying charge. His coach wanted him back in the van by six-thirty. Ms. Bekele, who had agreed to sponsor the play entry even though it wasn't debate, had told him only this: a moment from your own life, ten minutes on the stage, and the script has to be readable by strangers. He had never written a play. He had written cases, rebuttals, blocks of evidence about agricultural subsidies, and none of that helped him now.

The moment he chose was from October, which he had not planned to choose. His mother had come to a tournament for the first time and sat in the back of the room while he lost in quarterfinals, and afterward, in the parking lot, she had said something small that he still turned over. He wrote the scene in a rush, the two of them standing beside the car, and it came out visceral in a way his debate writing never did, the words closer to the ground. Then he sat looking at the pages and understood he had no idea how a script was supposed to look on the page. Prose dialogue ran together like a story, and a story was not a play.

Samira found him there with two granola bars and a bottle of water, which she set down before she said anything. She was waiting for the van too, and she had done the showcase the year before. "Who's in it?" she asked, reading over his shoulder. "Just the two of them," Michael said. "Me and my mom." Samira frowned at the page. "Okay, but she can't just stand there. What does she do while you're talking?" He hadn't thought about it. He added a line: she takes the keys out of her handbag. Then another: he looks at the ground. The words he added sat in the middle of the dialogue like stones in a stream, and he couldn't tell whether they belonged there or ruined it.

What he wanted, more than he could easily say, was for a stranger to be able to pick up his pages and stage his evening without him in the room. In debate, everything was explicit, every claim signposted, every clash delimited by the framework he announced in his first speech. A script seemed to want the opposite: instructions hidden inside something that looked like speech. He typed a trial line, his mother's line, and then after it, in the middle of the page, "He looks at the ground." Then he stared at it. If an actor read the page aloud, cold, how would they know that sentence was not something to say?

London, who had lost in octofinals and was wandering the halls, dropped into the seat across from Michael and pulled a printed script from his backpack, a photocopy of something for his drama class. Michael leaned over. He saw it at once: the spoken lines ran plain down the margin, and the actions sat apart from them, set off in italics and parentheses, so that anyone holding the page could tell at a glance which words were meant to be spoken and which were meant to be done. Stage directions in a script are usually set apart in italics or parentheses so actors and directors can tell them from spoken lines. Nobody had told him. He saw it in the format itself, and it was like being handed the key to a room he'd been pushing on.

He reformatted everything. (He looks at the ground.) (She takes the keys from her handbag.) The page organized itself into what was said and what was done, and when he read it back in his head, he heard the silence around the actions for the first time. It was almost seven. Samira read the new draft through once, slowly, while he watched her face and tried not to watch it. "The parking lot," she said finally. "It works. But you don't say who wins the argument." "Nobody wins," Michael said. "That's not what it's about." She considered this. "Then say that with the keys. Make her hold them and not give them back."

He wrote the ending twice. In the first version, his mother handed over the keys and the scene closed on a和解 he didn't believe in. In the second, she kept them, and the boy stood in the cold, and the audience would be left, he thought, exactly where he had been left. He didn't know which was truer. He emailed the second version with four minutes to spare, then sat with Samira and London eating the granola bars while the laptop's charge finally died.

Ms. Bekele found them at the van, and on the drive home she asked about the script. "It's about my mom," Michael said. "And me losing." She nodded and looked at the road. "Is that hard, people acting it?" He thought about the actor who would someday stand in a parking lot that wasn't his parking lot, holding keys that weren't his mother's keys, saying his words in a voice he'd never heard. "Maybe," he said. "I'll find out at rehearsal." Samira, in the seat behind him, passed forward the last of the water bottle, and he drank it as the highway lights came on.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: A 2005 study by Justin Kruger, Nicholas Epley and colleagues found that email writers overestimate how well readers will pick up their intended tone, such as sarcasm or seriousness.
story:
The volunteer office smelled of toner and old coffee, and Ava had been answering the hotline for two hours before the printer jammed and gave her something else to hate. She was filling in for the summer between graduation and moving into her dorm, three mornings a week, logging calls about utility assistance and food vouchers. The new coordinator, who started on Monday, had sent everyone an email that morning titled "Protocol for Written Correspondence," and Ava had replied within four minutes. She'd typed, "Wow, I love being managed by a bulleted list," pressed send, and gone back to the printer. It had seemed funny at the time. Leah, the other volunteer on shift, had laughed at her screen without looking up.

At noon the coordinator called her into the back room. The office had one window, half-blocked by a filing cabinet, and the coordinator stood beside it with a printed copy of Ava's email in her hand, actually printed, the way a person holds evidence.

"Is there something about the protocol that concerns you," the coordinator said. Not a question at the end. Ava looked at the paper and saw the sentence again, plain and cold in twelve-point font, and understood that it was not cold at all, that it had never been cold, that she had heard a voice where there was only text.

"I was joking," Ava said. "About the bullets. It was a joke."

"Then say so." The coordinator set the page face-down on the cabinet. "This is your file from now on. Everything in writing counts."

In the break room afterward, Ava sat with her sandwich untouched and her phone out, typing and deleting apologies. Leah came in and dropped a granola bar on the table. "I heard through the wall," Leah said. "You want the number for the draft where you say sorry twice? Because you already wrote it twice."

"I don't know how to make it sound like me without sounding rude." Ava turned the phone toward her. "If I write it flat, I sound like a machine. If I write it like I talk, she thinks I'm mocking her."

Leah pulled out her own phone and scrolled for a while, chewing. "Okay, hold on. My psych textbook had this thing. There was a study in 2005, Justin Kruger and Nicholas Epley, and other researchers, and they found that email writers overestimate how well readers will pick up their intended tone. Like sarcasm, or seriousness. You think they'll hear the joke. They don't."

Ava read over Leah's shoulder, but Leah had only the textbook's summary, a few lines in a sidebar about egocentrism, and Ava wanted more than a sidebar. She spent her lunch hour finding the paper itself, skimming the abstract while the office fridge hummed behind her. It was worse than she'd thought, and also a relief. The problem wasn't that she was a terrible person. The problem was structural. Email stripped out her voice, her half-smile, the pitch that turned a complaint into a tease, and the reader filled the silence with whatever mood she was already in. A new coordinator, trying to establish herself, would hear mockery. Anyone might.

But knowing the mechanism, or at least knowing the finding, did not tell her what to do next. She sat with that for a moment, the sandwich going dry in its wrapper. She could write formally, the way the protocol asked, and sound like nobody. She could write warmly and risk it being read as flippant again. Or she could do something third: write the formal structure and then name her own tone inside the email, out loud, so the reader didn't have to guess. She didn't know if it would work. She knew the study said her confidence was untrustworthy, which was an awkward foundation for any plan.

She drafted while the afternoon calls came in. A garrulous man on the hotline spent eleven minutes describing his landlord before getting to the leak, and she took notes and kept her voice level, the way the training binder said, and noticed she was doing in speech what she had failed to do in writing: signaling, constantly, that she was on his side. When he finally said, "You're the first person who didn't treat me like an idiot," she recalibrated something in her head, quietly, without ceremony.

The draft went through four versions. The first was stiff enough to embarrass her. The second was too sorry. The third, she showed to Leah, who said, "It sounds like a hostage letter." On the fourth, Ava wrote the opening sentence plainly: "I want to apologize for my earlier reply, and to be clear about tone, since I've learned that doesn't always come through in email: I was joking, and badly." Then she stated what she'd actually meant, agreed to follow the protocol, and asked one real question about how the office preferred written correspondence with clients. She read it aloud in her head, heard where it dragged, cut the dragging parts. She pressed send at 4:40 and went home without an answer.

The next morning Mr. Choi, the retired teacher who volunteered on Fridays and folded the pamphlets with surgical precision, was in the front room when Ava arrived. "The coordinator left this for you," he said, and nodded at her desk. It was a printed reply, one paragraph, acknowledging the apology and answering her question about client correspondence, with a suggestion that the two of them revise the client template together next week. Ava read it twice. It was formal, but there was a sentence near the end, about bulleted lists, that she was almost certain was a joke, though she couldn't completely tell, and she understood, standing there, that she never would be able to completely tell, that this was the tax on the form. She laughed anyway, at what she hoped was the right place, and Mr. Choi looked over at her from the pamphlets.

"Good news?" he asked.

"Undecided," Ava said, and sat down to open the template file.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: In his 1961 book What Is History?, E. H. Carr described history as 'an unending dialogue between the present and the past'.
story:
The essay was due at eight the next morning, and Daniel had chosen, with eleven hours to go, to change his topic entirely. Ms. Delgado had approved his original plan, a tidy paper on the harbor monument downtown, in which he would explain what it meant and why it mattered. But that afternoon his grandfather had stood in front of the thing with his hands in his coat pockets and said it honored the men who built the harbor, while Gary, who had walked over with Daniel to kill time, said it was obviously about the strike, about the workers who'd been shot, and that the plaque was a whitewash. Two people, one block of granite, and they had argued the whole walk home in the petulant way grown men argue when neither can win.

So now Daniel sat in the library at a carrel near the window, where the radiator ticked and smelled faintly of scorched dust, with three books open in front of him and forty minutes until closing. The first book, published in 1974, called the monument a tribute to civic progress. The second, from 1998, called the same stone an emblem of suppressed labor unrest. Neither mentioned the other. He kept turning back to the photographs, identical in both books, the same dedicatory crowd, the same ribbon, and he could not make the two captions agree about what the photograph showed.

Jillian was at the next carrel, allegedly studying for calculus, actually eating sunflower seeds one at a time and watching him rearrange his books. "You look like a man losing a fight with a filing cabinet," she said.

"I don't know which one to use. One of them has to be lying."

"Or both of them are telling the truth badly." She spat a shell into her palm with great dignity. "Look, if you hate it that much, write about why they can't agree. That seems more interesting anyway."

The reference shelf was behind him, and it was there, while pretending to search for a style manual, that Daniel found the Carr. It was a small gray book, thinner than either of his monument histories, its cover soft with handling. He read the first few pages standing up, then carried it back to the carrel and read the passage twice more, slowly, because the closing bell was going to ring in twenty minutes and he wanted to get it down before it dissolved the way library things did. In his 1961 book What Is History?, E. H. Carr had described history as "an unending dialogue between the present and the past."

He copied it out, then sat and ruminated on it longer than he could afford to. The 1974 book had been written by a man whose father, judging by the acknowledgments, had worked in the harbor office. The 1998 author thanked a union archive. Neither was simply wrong. Each had gone to the past with a different question, and the past, being a heap of receipts and photographs and half-remembered grievances, had answered each of them partially. His grandfather and Gary had done the same thing at the foot of the monument, each holding a question the stone could not refuse to answer.

It was not, he decided, the same as saying anything goes. Jillian liked to take that route, some flimsy everything-is-a-perspective rationalism that let her conclude whatever she'd already wanted to conclude before she started thinking. The sources were partial, not fictional; the plaque's date was a fact, the shooting was a fact, and the argument was about which facts carried the weight. But the argument itself, the disagreement, was not a failure to be cleaned up. It was the actual machinery of the thing.

The lights above the far stacks blinked, the library's polite way of saying get out. Daniel closed the Carr and slid it toward the return cart, then opened his notebook and wrote a new first paragraph, crossing out the old thesis so hard the pencil tore a little. Somewhere behind him a security guard wheeled a rubber bin past the periodicals, and the automatic door at the entrance exhaled its cold night air across the lobby.

Jillian zipped her bag and waited, uncharacteristically patient, while he gathered the two monument books. "So what's the paper about now?"

"About why my grandfather and you and Gary can all look at the same rock and see different centuries." He shouldered his bag. "And about whether that's a problem or just what history is."

"Which is it?"

He held the door for her, and the cold hit them both. "Ask me tomorrow at eight."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, every new employee must complete Section 1 of Form I-9, which verifies identity and permission to work, no later than their first day of paid work.
story:
Jordan got the job on a Tuesday, which felt appropriate, because Tuesday was the most ordinary day of the week and the job itself was ordinary: scooping ice cream at the shop two blocks from his house, weekends and two evenings, minimum wage. The manager, a tired man named only in Jordan's head as the manager, had shaken his hand and then handed him a form and a pen, which seemed to reverse the order of celebration and paperwork. "You fill out Section 1 yourself," the man said. "It's the I-9. It verifies your identity and your permission to work. You have to have it done no later than your first day of paid work, so that's Saturday, ten a.m." Jordan said sure, folded the form into his back pocket, and rode home with the paper sweating against him all the way up the hill.

At the kitchen table he spread it out under the light. His mother had inculcated in him certain domestic rituals over the years, among them that important documents were to be flattened, read entirely, and never signed at a restaurant table, and he obeyed all three now. Section 1 wanted his name, his address, his citizenship status, and then, in a box that had a way of looking larger the longer he stared at it, either a Social Security number or a statement that he didn't have one. He knew his number. He had memorized it in seventh grade for reasons he no longer remembered. What he could not produce was the card itself, because the box on the form said, in small gray print, that if he used the number, he might have to show the card.

He went to the hall closet where his mother kept a metal box of family records, the kind of box that appeared in every household he had ever visited, as if issued by the state along with birth certificates. His mother was at work until six. The box contained his vaccination records, a lease from an apartment they'd left in 2013, a photo of his grandfather standing in montane forest somewhere in Colorado, squinting under pines, and no Social Security card.

He texted Rio first, because Rio was always awake and always entertaining. "do i legally exist," Jordan typed, and attached a picture of the form. Rio called him within a minute. "Bro, that's an I-9," Rio said, in the tone of someone identifying a bird. "Tala did one at the garden center." This was Rio's project lately, getting everyone employed, partly out of friendship and partly because Rio had applied to the same ice cream shop, been passed over, and now wanted a full report on what he was missing. "Ask her about the card thing. Also ask if they let you eat the broken cones. This is critical intelligence."

Tala answered on the second ring, and Jordan could hear the garden center's sprinklers in the background. "Section 1 is just your part," she said. "You fill it out, you sign it, and it has to be done by your first day of paid work. Not the interview, the actual paid work. They check your documents after, that's their section." She had learned this the way she learned everything, by asking a cashier named Doreen a series of questions so organized that Doreen eventually asked if she was from the government. "The card doesn't have to be the card, though. Passport works. Birth certificate plus something with a photo. Doreen said the list is on the form."

There was a list, on the back, and Jordan found it now, Lists of Acceptable Documents, which sounded like a title from the driest library in the world. The passport was at his father's apartment, across town, in a drawer his father described as "the important drawer," a drawer so famously disorganized that Jordan had once found a passport sitting on top of a 2009 tax return and a manual for a grill they no longer owned. He called his father, who said, with genuine surprise, "You're working? Since when?" and then, recovering, "I can look tonight. Or you could come look. I made soup."

Jordan sat for a moment with the form and the phone and the metal box. In Ms. Do's class last spring there had been a unit she called, with apparent pleasure, epistemology, which as far as Jordan could tell meant asking not what you knew but how you knew it, and he had mostly enjoyed the arguments about it without ever expecting it to be useful. But here it was, useful: he knew his Social Security number, confidently, the way he knew his own birthday, and yet that confidence had no paper behind it, no card, nothing a manager could look at. There was knowing and there was proving, and the form, he understood, lived entirely in the second country. His mother knew things the first way, by heart, and had inculcated that habit in him too; she could recite account numbers like poetry. The world of the form wanted the metal box, and the metal box had let him down.

So he did both. He wrote his number in the box, printed his name, checked the citizenship box, and signed Section 1 at the kitchen table with his mother's good pen, dated it, and set it flat under the sugar bowl so it wouldn't curl. Then he texted his father: coming for soup, bringing the form, need the passport from the drawer. His father replied with a thumbs up and a photo of the soup, which was aggressively orange.

On the bus across town he read the form one more time, not because he expected it to change but because his mother's habits had become his habits, and he found he liked the small formality of it, the sense that a country had thought about the moment a boy first got paid and had decided that the moment should have a shape. His father's passport turned up in the important drawer in under four minutes, a record, and his father photographed Jordan holding it, sent the photo to Jordan's mother with the caption "professional," and ladled soup.

Saturday morning Jordan arrived at ten, not ten past, with the form in a folder and the passport in his mother's zippered document pouch, which she had handed over at the door with the ceremony of someone lending out a violin. The manager took the folder, glanced at Section 1, initialed something, and said, "Documents?" Jordan produced the passport. "Good," the manager said. "Some kid last summer showed up with nothing and we had to send him home. Now grab an apron." Behind the counter, Rio was already there, sitting on a milk crate, wearing a shirt with the shop's logo, holding a spoon. "They called me Friday," Rio said. "Someone quit. I'm your coworker. Also I've eaten three broken cones and I have findings."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen is exothermic, so low temperatures favour more ammonia at equilibrium, but industrial plants run hotter because the reaction is too slow when cold.
story:
The kettle had boiled twice already and nobody had made tea with it, which struck Cohen as a kind of metaphor he refused to pursue, because the quiz opened online at seven and closed at nine, and metaphor would not help him with equilibrium.

Marilie had claimed the good chair and spread her notes across the kitchen table like a general deploying forces. Etienne sat on the counter with his ankles crossed, eating cereal out of the box, which he did whenever he was nervous and wanted to appear casual about it. Cohen stood at the stove because standing helped him think, and because from the stove he could see the laptop, the clock on the microwave, and the window where the streetlight was coming on too early, which did not augur well for the weather or for his concentration.

"Le Chatelier," Marilie said. "Say it back to me."

"A system at equilibrium, when you disturb it, shifts to oppose the disturbance."

"Good. So you add heat to a reaction. Which way does it go?"

"It depends," Cohen said, and Etienne said, into the cereal box, "That's the most Cohen answer in the history of answers."

"It depends on whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Heat is a product or a reactant. You add a product, the system consumes it. You remove it, the system makes more."

Marilie pointed her pen at him. "So a reaction that releases heat."

"Exothermic. Add heat and it shifts backward, away from the products. Cool it and it shifts forward, toward more product." He said it and, saying it, felt the small tectonic settling of a concept into place, the way a puzzle piece goes in and takes the whole board with it. "Cool an exothermic reaction and you get more product at equilibrium. That's the rule."

"Then why," Etienne said, "does the Haber plant run hot? My uncle works at one, he says the vessels run way hotter than room temperature. If cold gives you more ammonia, why would a factory choose a temperature that gives less product? Are they stupid? Are entire nations stupid?"

The kettle ticked as it cooled. Cohen turned it off, though it was already off, and turned it back off again.

"They run it hot because the reaction is too slow when cold," he said slowly. "That's the whole thing. That's the twist."

"What twist?"

"The twist inside the rule. Cold gives you more ammonia at equilibrium, sure, but you'd wait basically forever to get it. So they run hotter, get less ammonia at equilibrium, but get it faster." He was talking faster now, one hand flat on the counter. "The principle tells you where the equilibrium sits. It says nothing about how fast you get there. Two completely different questions. One's about the destination, one's about the speed."

Marilie had stopped writing. "That's not in our notes."

"It's in the textbook, page two-something, in a box nobody reads. I read it last night because I couldn't sleep."

"You couldn't sleep so you read the boxes."

"The boxes are where the honest stuff lives. The chapter gives you the clean rule and then the box says, actually, in the real world, the clean rule gets overruled by time." He pulled the milk from the fridge and set it in front of Etienne, who took the hint and made actual cereal. "It's like an epistemology problem," Cohen went on, and Etienne groaned, and Cohen kept going anyway. "No, listen. How do you know what you know? In the chapter you know it because the rule is elegant. In the box you know it because someone had to make a ton of ammonia cheaply and the elegant rule failed them. I trust the box more. But I can't fully prove the box. I've never run a plant."

"Six forty," Marilie said. "Twenty minutes."

They drilled. Nitrogen and hydrogen, ammonia, exothermic, Cohen repeating the pairing until it was rhythm: low temperature favours more ammonia at equilibrium, plants run hot anyway because cold is too slow. Etienne asked it four times from four angles, the way he did before a free throw, and by the fourth time Cohen could answer while pouring water for the tea he finally made.

At seven the quiz opened. Question three read: A reactor makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen. Explain why an industrial plant operates at an elevated temperature even though a lower temperature would give a higher yield of ammonia at equilibrium.

Etienne made a sound like a kettle. Marilie laughed, once, startled. Cohen read it twice, then typed, and it was strange to feel grateful to a question, and stranger to know the gratitude came from a night he'd spent sleepless with a box in a textbook. He wrote: the reaction is exothermic, so low temperature favours more ammonia at equilibrium; plants run hotter because the reaction is too slow when cold. He read it over. He did not add anything. The clock on the microwave said 7:14.

"Question five," Etienne said from the counter. "It's asking about the epistemology thing. The one about how you know a model works."

"Finish your cereal," Cohen said, and kept typing.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: The Seder plate holds maror, bitter herbs such as horseradish, which are eaten to recall the bitterness of slavery in Egypt.
story:
Matthew had the Haggadah open on the kitchen table and the phone wedged against his shoulder when his grandmother's voice announced, from three hundred miles away, that this year it was his turn. "Your grandfather led it for forty years," she said. "Your father mangles the Hebrew. You're the one who actually reads." She said it the way she said everything, as though the matter had been settled sometime before he was born, and honestly he was a little flattered and a lot terrified, because in twelve days his aunts and uncles and four cousins would be at his parents' table expecting a Seder led from start to finish by an eighteen-year-old whose entire religious education had ended at bar mitzvah, an event his uncle still called "the pasta incident."

He decided to practice in public, on the theory that if he could survive strangers, he could survive family. The spring cultural festival on the riverfront had a row of tables where people sold dumplings and henna and informational pamphlets, and Ms. Castillo, who taught across the hall from his old history classroom, had offered him a spot next to her quesadilla stand for a demonstration table. He set out a cloth, a Seder plate borrowed from his mother's cabinet, and a handwritten sign that read ASK ME ANYTHING, which within twenty minutes he regretted deeply, because the first question was "Is that a very small frisbee?" and the second was "Why is there a shank bone on your plate, are you a wizard?"

Brenna showed up around noon with two lemonades and no knowledge whatsoever, which turned out to be the most useful thing anyone brought all day. "Okay," she said, pointing at the pile of pale root on the corner of the plate, "explain the raw horseradish, because I watched a man take a bite of that an hour ago and I thought he was being punished." That part he actually knew. "It's called maror," he said. "Bitter herbs. Everyone eats it at the Seder on purpose, to recall the bitterness of slavery in Egypt." She stared at him. "You eat awful food to remember something awful?" "Basically." "That's deranged," she said, and then, after a second, "No, wait, I get it. It's like my mom making me look at the picture of my broken arm every time I say the skateboard was a good idea." A man at the next table bought a pamphlet out of pity.

Milo arrived with news, which was how Milo always arrived. He had gone to the supermarket for Matthew, since the family horseradish was apparently in a freezer in a house in a state where Matthew's uncle had recently moved, and the text he sent was a small catastrophe: "they have NO horseradish. zero. the root guy at the farmers market isn't here. i am holding six boxes of matzo and a beet and i feel like a fraud." Matthew read it twice, and the panic arrived on schedule, subterranean at first, a low hum under the festival noise, then surfacing fast. No maror, no Seder, no leading anything.

He did what he'd watched his grandfather do for years, which was make a list. Horseradish sauce in a jar: Milo had checked, the supermarket was out, because apparently everyone in town was hosting a Seder simultaneously, a conspiracy he chose not to examine. Romaine lettuce: traditional, technically acceptable, and available at the gas station three blocks away if he ran. "Romaine," he told Brenna, and she said, "Lettuce as a substitute for punishment? That's an indemnity if I've ever seen one. You're compensating your guests for the suffering they were promised." He laughed harder than the joke deserved, out of relief, and then jogged the three blocks in the heat and came back with two heads of romaine and a sunburn he'd describe later as "a tan."

The problem that actually mattered surfaced during the run-through. Ms. Castillo, wiping down her griddle between customers, asked him a question no one at the festival had thought to ask and everyone at the table would: "So when you lead it, are you following the book, or are you following your grandfather?" He stood there holding lettuce in the sun. The honest answer was that he had been trying to do his grandfather's Seder with a teenage boy's voice coming out of it, and neither of those things absolved him from choosing. The book said one order of songs; his grandfather had sung them a different way, slower, with a joke about the youngest cousin hidden in the third verse. He couldn't have both. Or maybe, he thought, turning the romaine over in his hands, he could, but he'd have to decide line by line instead of inheriting it whole, which was more work and somehow more his.

Twelve days later the table was set, the candles were lit, and the cousins were already fighting about who got to steal the afikoman. Matthew stood, took a breath, poured the first cup, and started the way the book said, word for word, steady. When they reached the maror, he handed the plate to Brenna, who was there as the official first-time guest and unofficial videographer. "It's bitter on purpose," he told her quietly. "Slavery in Egypt. That's the whole point." She took the smallest permissible piece of horseradish, chewed it, and turned a color he would tease her about for years, and when the singing came he slowed it down, put the joke in the third verse, and heard his uncle's laugh come from somewhere deep and satisfied, like a kettle finally on. Milo raised his glass of grape juice and said, "To lettuce."

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: The last time a British monarch refused royal assent to a bill was in 1708, when Queen Anne vetoed the Scottish Militia Bill.
story:
The city council chamber smelled of floor polish and old coffee, and Megan had claimed a seat near the aisle so she could see the whole horseshoe of desks. The council had lent the chamber to the youth model parliament for the evening, one real aide had told them, because the building stood empty on Thursdays anyway. Her bill, the one she had drafted three times in a notebook with a cracked spine, was second on the order paper.

"Point of order," said Frank, who sat in the Speaker's chair with unearned authority. "We proceed to committee of the whole on Bill C-3."

Megan's clause lived in Bill C-3. Weekend transit fares capped at two dollars for anyone under eighteen, written after the spring she had spent riding the 41 bus to her mother's night shifts because the full fare ate her allowance by the third week of the month. She had walked the language to Raphaelle first, in the school library, where Raphaelle had read it twice and said, "It's clean, but the clause about enforcement is vague, and they'll gut it." Megan had revised anyway, keeping the enforcement vague on purpose, because the precise version would have named inspectors, and inspectors cost money, and money was where bills went to die.

The committee stage took forty minutes she would not get back. A boy from another school moved to strike the fare cap entirely, calling it "doctrinaire meddling in the market," and Megan stood twice at her desk to defend it, hands flat on the wood so they wouldn't shake. Raphaelle, seated across the aisle as an opposition member, rose against her own friend's bill on the enforcement clause, and Megan felt the betrayal before she understood the tactic. Without enforcement, the cap was a wish. With it, the committee could claim the bill was unworkable. Raphaelle was making her choose between a hollow law and a dead one.

"Amendment," Megan said, when the chair recognized her. "The cap applies to any fare machine that accepts a youth card. No inspectors. The system enforces itself." It was a compromise neither side liked, which was, she was beginning to suspect, the actual signature of a law.

Debate in the full house was shorter and meaner. Someone called the bill socialism; someone else called its opponents charlatans who rode subsidised parking every day of their lives. Megan listened, and what she heard was that most of the room had not read past the title, that they had habituated themselves to voting on the first line and the mood of the room, and she stopped trying to persuade them and started counting heads instead. She needed twelve. She had, by her count while pretending to review her notes, ten, and then the boy who had moved the strike caught her eye and shrugged. Eleven.

The vote carried, thirteen to nine. Megan sat down too fast and knocked her pen to the floor.

Then Frank stood, removed the paper crown he had worn since the role assignment, and said, "As Lieutenant Governor, I refuse royal assent to this bill."

The chamber exploded into argument before Megan had even picked up her pen. Half the room believed him; the other half shouted him down; Frank held the crown in one hand like a gavel and would not sit. Megan pulled out her phone and typed fast, thumb sliding on the screen, and found it in a municipal wiki entry and then again in a better source, the same words in both places.

She stood. "Point of information. The last time a British monarch refused royal assent to a bill was in 1708, when Queen Anne vetoed the Scottish Militia Bill."

"Then it can happen," Frank said.

"It hasn't happened since," Megan said. "Three hundred years. You can refuse, on paper. Nobody does."

Frank looked at the crown, then at the order paper, then at Ms. Costa, the teacher supervising at the back, who had been watching the whole exchange with her arms folded and said nothing at all, which Megan understood to be the point. The room was quiet in the way a real chamber must be quiet, everyone waiting to see whether power would be used or merely worn.

Frank set the crown back on his head. "I assent."

They made her acting Lieutenant Governor for the final bill of the evening, because Frank's bus left early and someone had to hold the crown. The final bill was the parking one, the one that had been kicking around the model parliament since October, and Megan read it through while the debate rolled over her. Buried in clause six, in language almost nobody read: municipal parking revenues could be redirected to cover shortfalls anywhere in the transit budget, at council's discretion, and nothing in any other bylaw, including Bill C-3, could be read to constrain that discretion.

It had passed while she was counting heads. It had passed, she realized, in the same lopsided, unread, first-line vote she had spent the whole evening quietly exploiting.

The Speaker asked whether she assented.

Megan looked at Raphaelle, who was not looking at her, and put down the bill. "Before I answer," she said, "can the mover tell me what clause six does?"

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Holding static stretches for a long time, about 60 seconds or more per muscle, right before explosive activity can briefly reduce strength and power, so many programs warm up with dynamic movement.
story:
The rink was empty except for the mite practice sharing one end, and John spread his notebook on the bleachers where the cold came up through the steel. He had promised Mr. Rosen he would bring a weekly training plan to Thursday's meeting, and so far he had seven nearly identical pages of scribbled arrows. In the first week he had written the word "hard" eleven times and the word "rest" once, in the margin, with a question mark after it.

Lilly came up the steps with two hot chocolates and set one beside the notebook without asking. She played defence on the girls' team and had opinions about everything, including his arrows. She read while he drank, and he watched her face do the thing it did when she found a problem: a small flattening around the mouth, like ice before it cracked.

"Tuesday, hard. Wednesday, hard. Thursday, game, then hard after," she said. "Where's the part where your legs come back?"

"That's what the stretching is for," John said. "Before everything. My brother's whole routine. He holds each stretch forever, like a minute at least, sixty seconds, feels like a punishment. Then he goes." His brother ran the 400 for the college team, and John had copied the routine the way an acolyte copies liturgy, without asking what any of it was for.

Lilly turned the notebook sideways. "My brother did that at a meet in the spring. Held his hamstring stretch on the line till his name got called, over a minute easy. Then he ran his worst race of the season. Said his legs felt like they belonged to somebody slower." She shrugged. "He switched his whole warm-up after. Skips, leg swings, walking lunges, all moving stuff. He calls it dynamic."

"Moving stuff," John said.

"Dynamic," she said again. "As opposed to the holding kind. Static. He read it somewhere and made me quiz him on it."

John wrote the word down, and under it, a question he didn't say out loud, which was whether the holding kind was bad or only bad right before, whether it calcified into harm or only borrowed against the first minutes of a shift. He knew from his own body that long holds loosened something in a hip that had been locked since September. But the first stride of a game wanted snap, not looseness. Those were two different goods, and he could not make them the same by writing harder.

At the far end of the rink, Samara was running her own warm-up along the boards, having finished with the mites. She wore a gray hoodie with a cormorant stitched across the back, wings spread, some pelagic bird a continent away from this landlocked county, and she did high knees the length of the blue line and back, then leg swings holding the glass. When she crossed the ice to the benches she saw the notebook open and came up the steps without being invited.

"Is that the program?" she said. "Rosen said you were doing one." She sat, pulled the pen out of John's hand, and drew a grid on a clean page. Seven columns. In the first column she wrote the days. In the third she wrote REST and boxed it twice. "Whole day. Not a light day. A day."

"That feels like giving up a day," John said.

"That's the day you get stronger," Samara said. "The work breaks you down and the day off builds it back. My physio used to say rest was the exercise you do lying down." She tapped the other boxes. "And warm-ups go before each session, dynamic before ice time, and the long holding stretches after, when the power part is already over and nobody's asking your legs for anything."

John looked at the grid. It was simpler than his arrows and it made a claim his arrows never had, that the week was a shape, that rest and work were load-bearing the same way. He thought of his brother flat on the start line and understood, suddenly, that the routine he had inherited was built for a body and a sport that were not his. He could keep the parts that served him. He did not have to keep the rest out of loyalty.

They stayed until the zamboni came out and the mites were herded toward the parking lot. John copied the grid into fresh ink, moved his long holds to the end of each day, wrote dynamic before every ice session, and left Wednesday empty except for the boxed word. He underlined it once, then stopped, because Samara was holding the door to the rink open and the cold outside was already coming through it.

"Thursday, then," she said. "Tell Rosen the rest day was my idea and I want royalties."

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: False friends are words that look alike in two languages but differ in meaning; Spanish 'embarazada' means pregnant, not embarrassed.
story:
The topic was drawn from a coffee can on Mr. Chea's desk, folded slips of paper that smelled faintly of grounds, and Mason unfolded his to find the words "Redes sociales" in pencil. Social media. Five minutes, entirely in Spanish, in front of a class that would grade him on argument, fluency and something Mr. Chea called aplomo, which Mason understood to mean standing like a man while his brain emptied itself through his ears.

He had two positions and no way to choose between them. His mother, who read three newspapers before breakfast, thought social media was pernicious, eating away at attention and patience like damp through a wall. His older sister, who ran a small jewelry business from her phone, credited it with her livelihood. Both were right about real things. Mason had spent the week writing notecards that argued past each other, and now it was Wednesday, and Friday was the debate, and his stack of cards smelled like the coffee can.

"Pick both," said Kristian at lunch, stealing a fry. "Say the platform is the problem and the people are the answer. Teachers love that."

"That's not a position, that's a shrug."

"It's a synthesis," said Heath, who had taken philosophy electives and enjoyed deploying them. "Historicize it. Like, social media isn't new, gossip isn't new, the marketplace isn't new. Then argue about what's actually new."

"Stop using my paper as a napkin," Mason said, but he copied the word historicize onto a clean card, then crossed it out because he couldn't conjugate anything that fancy in Spanish, and wrote instead that humans had always loved talking about each other.

Friday came with rain beading on the classroom windows and the smell of somebody's vape ghosting through the vents. Mason was fourth. The first speaker, a girl who had lived in Madrid for a year, argued that social media connected immigrants to their families, and Mason felt his throat tighten because she made it sound so easy, her sentences falling into place like folded laundry. The second speaker was Heath, who froze for thirty seconds and then said "estoy embarazado" and the class dissolved. Even Mr. Chea put his face in his hands, shoulders shaking.

"What did I say?" Heath whispered, sitting down red.

Kristian leaned across the aisle, delighted beyond all restraint. "You announced you were pregnant. Embarazada means pregnant, not embarrassed."

"There's a name for those," the Madrid girl said from the front row, still laughing. "False friends. Words that look alike in two languages but mean different things."

Heath turned a deeper shade and muttered something about Spanish being out to get him personally, and Mason, waiting for his turn with his cards sweating in his hand, watched Mr. Chea write false friends on the board without further comment, apparently for Monday's lesson. But Mason was not really watching the board. He was looking at his own top card, on which he had written, with great confidence, "La gente está embarazada por las noticias falsas." People are pregnant by fake news. He crossed it out so hard the pencil tore the paper, then printed "avergonzada" above it, which he hoped meant embarrassed and had no time to doubt.

When his five minutes came, he stood, planted his feet the way his sister planted hers when arguing with suppliers, and made his argument in Spanish that was simple and sometimes wrong in its grammar but never in its direction. People had always talked about each other, he said; the market, the plaza, the letters; what was new was the speed and the size. Then the turn: the danger was not the tool but the use, though the tool made the bad use easy, and maybe a person could hold both of those at once without falling over. He heard his own hesitation on the last sentence and let it stand. Some of the class nodded. One boy in the back, a reactionary about all technology, shook his head slowly the whole time, and Mason found he didn't mind, that the shaking head felt almost like applause for the parts he had gotten right.

Afterward, while the next speaker arranged her cards, Heath slid into the empty desk beside him. "How do you know what you said was actually Spanish?"

"I don't. Some of it might have been pregnant."

Heath laughed into his sleeve, and Mr. Chea, passing back papers, paused at Mason's desk long enough to tap the torn card where embarazada lay crossed out under its correction. "A vergonzada," he said, as if tasting it. "Well survived."

Mason looked down at the card, at the word he had gotten wrong and the word he had guessed at, both of them sitting there in pencil, neither one apologizing.

"What did I get on it?" he asked.

"Monday," said Mr. Chea, and moved on toward the windows and the rain.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: US food safety agencies say chicken is safely cooked when its internal temperature reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.
story:
The market opened at eight, and by half past, Elijah had already made two circuits of the stalls without buying anything. His mother had left for the hospital shift before he woke, and on the kitchen table she'd propped a note in her slanted handwriting: "Dinner is yours tonight. Chicken in the fridge. Dad home at seven." He'd read it three times over toast, and each reading had adumbrated the same problem: he had never cooked a whole meal in his life, and tonight he would have to.

At Mr. Murphy's stall he stopped in front of trays of greens, mainly to look like someone with a plan. Mr. Murphy, who had sold his family tomatoes for years, nodded at Elijah's empty basket. "First time cooking?" he asked, and Elijah admitted it was, that it was chicken and whatever he could figure out to put beside it. "Then take the carrots and the little potatoes," Mr. Murphy said, bagging them before Elijah could object, "and don't overpay at the next stall for bread, they're charging for the basket." He slipped a bruised but fine-looking lemon in with the carrots and waved off the extra dollar Elijah tried to hand him.

Lillian found him near the honey stand, carrying a paper cone of strawberries she'd bought for no reason except that it was Saturday. When he told her about the dinner, his voice flattening under the weight of it, she laughed in a way that made the weight seem smaller. "My mom made me cook every Thursday senior year," she said. "You'll be fine. The only thing that actually matters is the chicken." She pulled out her phone, typed for a moment, and turned the screen toward him so he could read it himself: "US food safety agencies say chicken is safely cooked when its internal temperature reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer." She forwarded it to him. "My mom made me memorize it. Do you have a thermometer?"

He didn't know. He'd never had reason to look. At home, he ransacked the drawers beside the stove, a morass of rubber bands, takeout menus, birthday candles, and a corkscrew nobody admitted to owning, and found nothing that resembled a thermometer. He texted Lillian a photo of the chaos and she replied with a single crying-laughing face, then, a minute later: "check the drawer under the oven, that's where mine hides." It was there, a slim metal probe in a plastic sleeve, apparently purchased by his father at some point and then buried. He washed it and set it on the counter like an instrument he now had to learn.

Ariella, who had taken a food science elective and never let anyone forget it, messaged him while the potatoes were boiling: "heard from Lillian you're doing chicken. promise me you're not going to guess." He sent back a photo of the thermometer lying beside the raw breasts with their lemon and salt, and she replied, "a man of science," followed by three exclamation points, and then, more seriously: "the thermometer goes in the thickest part, don't touch the bone or the pan." He wrote "thickest part, no bone" on the back of his mother's note and set it where he could see it.

The ancillary worries, the sides and the timing and whether rice would have been better than potatoes, crowded in anyway, but the chicken itself became strangely simple. He browned the breasts in the pan because a video had said to, slid them into the oven, and when they looked done, golden and firm, he nearly took them out on faith. Instead he pushed the probe into the thickest part of the largest breast, careful to avoid the bone, and watched the numbers climb: 140, 151, then a pause so long he opened the oven door to check that the display hadn't frozen. It read 165. He took them out, and the thermometer came away clean.

His father came through the door at ten past seven, loosening a tie, and stopped in the kitchen doorway when he smelled it. Elijah plated the chicken, the carrots glazed with the honey Lillian had insisted he buy, the potatoes split and steaming, and set his father's plate down first. His father cut into the breast, paused, and looked up at him.

"I used the thermometer," Elijah said. "Dad, did you know chicken is safely cooked when its internal temperature reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer?"

His father chewed, swallowed, and pushed his chair back to reach the drawer under the oven, taking out the plastic sleeve Elijah had left lying there. "Bought that three years ago," he said. "Never used it once. Sit down before it gets cold."

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
