knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In periodized training, a season is divided into cycles; a microcycle, the smallest, usually lasts about one week.
story:
The clipboard felt heavier than it should have, given that it held only one sheet of paper. Christopher sat on the rolled mats at the far end of the gym, where the afternoon light came through the high windows in dusty bars, and looked at the grid he had drawn: seven columns, one for each day of the week, and beside each column a blank space waiting to be filled with something he did not yet know how to name.

Mr. Vogel had given the assignment that morning, and Christopher had spent the hours since alternately planning and avoiding it. Design a weekly training program for a sport, any sport, with rest days built in and a warm-up protocol specified. The coach had made it sound simple, the way he made everything sound simple, and had added that their grades depended less on ambition than on judgment. Christopher had chosen basketball, because he played it, and because he assumed he could cheat his way through on familiarity. He was discovering otherwise.

Lyric dropped onto the mat beside him with a squeak of sneakers and peered at the empty grid. "You've been staring at that since lunch," she said. "It's a schedule, not a hostage negotiation."

"It's the rest days that are the problem," Christopher said. "If I take Monday off and Thursday off, I feel like I'm writing laziness into the plan on purpose. Like I'm grading my own slacking and calling it strategy."

"That's the opposite of what rest is," Lyric said, but she said it lightly, not like a correction, more like she was handing him something to hold while he thought about it. She pulled her knees up and looked at the grid with him.

He had spent the previous evening arguing with his father about it, and the argument was still running in his head. His father's view was the old one, the one from his own playing days: you worked until the work was done, and rest was what happened when you collapsed. He hadn't meant to impugn anything as fancy as sports science; he simply didn't believe in it. Christopher hadn't pushed back hard, because he half agreed with the man, and because the part of him that disagreed couldn't yet say why in a full sentence.

Averie arrived with a basketball under one arm and an energy that filled the gym before she reached them. She was, in Mr. Vogel's dry phrasing, an obstreperous player, all noise and full-court presses, and she sat down now only because Lyric patted the mat. "Vogel wants these by Friday," she said. "Mine's done. It's got shooting drills every single day, because I need shooting drills every single day."

"You need rest days too," Christopher said.

"I rest in study hall."

Lyric laughed, and Averie grinned, and for a moment the problem felt smaller, shared around among three people instead of sitting on his chest. Christopher looked at his grid again, then at Averie's program, which she had produced from her backpack folded into quarters. Every day filled. Every day the same. It looked less like training and more like penance.

He went looking for the answer himself, which was how he ended up that evening in the school library with a coaching manual he'd found on the shelf next to the sports biographies, feeling faintly ridiculous until the book opened to a diagram that stopped him. A season, the book said, divided into cycles, nested inside each other like boxes. And there, at the smallest level, the level of one week, was a word he had never seen: microcycle. The book called the week-long cycle a microcycle. He read the line twice, then pulled out his phone and texted Lyric, because he could not stand to know it alone.

"You know coaches call a week of training a microcycle?" he said to her the next afternoon, back on the same mats, clipboard flat on his knees. "A whole season gets divided into cycles, and the smallest one is about one week. That's mine. That's what I'm building. It's not seven separate days. It's one unit, and the rest days are part of the unit, the same way the silence is part of a song."

"Okay," Lyric said slowly. "That actually makes sense. So where do the rests go?"

"That's the part I'm not sure about," he admitted. "Monday after a weekend game, probably, and Thursday, before Saturday. But I can't tell if Thursday should be a full rest or a light day with warm-ups and stretching only. The book gives principles, not answers." He filled in the columns anyway, writing warm-up sequences at the top of each active day, ankle work and dynamic stretches, the boring specifics he would never have bothered with a week ago. He left Thursday blank for the moment and looked at it.

In English class they had been reading about utilitarianism, the idea that the right choice was whatever produced the most good for the most people, and Christopher kept catching himself applying it to Thursday, weighing one hard practice against a week of tired legs, as though the days were people whose interests he had to balance. It didn't quite work, but it didn't quite not work either, and he decided he could live with that, the way he was learning to live with the blank column.

On Friday he handed the program in with Thursday marked as a full rest and a note in the margin saying he was not certain. Mr. Vogel read it at his desk, looked up, and did not say whether it was right. He looked at Averie's paper next, all seven days filled, and asked her one quiet question about the fourth quarter of a game in February. Averie said nothing for a long moment. Then she took her paper back, sat down on the bleachers, and began crossing out Wednesday.

"You could share the microcycle thing with her," Lyric whispered to Christopher. He nodded, got up, and walked over, clipboard under his arm, and sat down beside Averie in the empty gym.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In Arthur Aron's 1997 study, pairs of strangers took turns asking each other 36 questions that grew gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk.
story:
Nicole arrived at the scoop shop eleven minutes early, which she decided to reframe as punctuality plus a margin for disaster. She'd chosen the table by the window, the one with the good light and the wobbly leg she discovered only after setting down her phone, and now she was stuck with it, because changing tables at the last minute looked like the behavior of a person with a plan, and she did not want to be a person with a plan. She wanted to be a person who had wandered in, serenely, for a double scoop of pistachio.

Elijah arrived on time, which somehow unsettled her more than lateness would have. He was in the shirt from chemistry class, the green one with the ink stain shaped vaguely like Portugal, and he ordered a cone of something called Midnight Thunder without asking what was in it. "I trust a flavor with that kind of confidence," he said, and she laughed before she could decide whether the joke was good or just available.

For a while it went fine. They had known each other since sophomore year in the way you know a classmate, which is to say they could locate each other's lab goggles and opinions on the cafeteria pizza but had never once been alone together. The ice cream gave them something to do with their hands. They covered the weather, the unseasonable warmth, the rumor that the school was getting a second vending machine. Then, somewhere around the last third of her scoop, the conversation simply stopped, like a song that ends without a fade.

Nicole watched him roll his cone wrapper into a tight little cylinder and thought, with some alarm, that this was it, the part where a first date calcifies into an anecdote, the thing you mention to Maxym later with a shrug. She had texted Maxym beforehand and he had given her exactly one piece of advice, delivered with the gravity of a war general: don't interview him. An interview, Maxym said, is a date that's already lost.

"We could do questions," she said, before she could talk herself out of it. "Not interview questions. Like an experiment."

Elijah looked up, cone paused mid-lick, which gave him an unfairly comical gravity. "What kind of experiment?"

So she told him, because it was the one interesting thing she had. "There's this study. Arthur Aron, 1997. Pairs of strangers took turns asking each other thirty-six questions that got gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk." She had read about it at one in the morning three weeks ago, the way you read about everything, through a door in the internet you didn't remember opening. "I don't know if it works on people who already sort of know each other. That's not what he tested."

"Thirty-six," Elijah said. "That's a lot of questions."

"That's the point. It's not one good question. It's the pile."

He considered this, tapping the tabletop in the rhythm of a drum fill only he could hear. "What counts as gradually more personal? Like, do we start with my middle name and end with my deepest fear?"

"Basically, yes."

"Okay," he said. "But I get to skip one. One free skip, no penalty. Everyone deserves one question they don't answer on a first date at an ice cream shop."

"One skip," she agreed, and held out her hand, and they shook on it over the pistachio, which felt ridiculous and therefore right.

The first questions were, by design, nothing. Would you rather be famous or anonymous. What's a perfect day. The wobbly table rocked every time Elijah gestured, which he did constantly, so the whole arrangement had the rhythm of a slow boat. By question eleven, though, something had shifted, and she couldn't point to the moment it shifted, which bothered her in a faint, background way, the way a word you can't quite recall bothers you. He had told her about the year his grandmother moved in and the house got quieter and louder at the same time. She had told him about quitting piano, which she had never told anyone, because it sounded like nothing and felt like something.

"Question nineteen," Elijah said. "When did you last cry in front of another person?"

"Skipping my skip? Bold." She looked out the window instead of at him. Two little kids were having what appeared to be a formal dispute over a sprinkles situation, and their mother was conducting negotiations with the weary patience of a UN delegate. "In front of another person. Last spring. My dad, after the college emails started coming. Not the good ones."

He didn't say sorry, which she appreciated more than she could have said. Instead: "Mine was at my grandmother's funeral, and I was mostly crying because everyone kept telling me it was okay to cry, which made it impossible to stop."

The shop had gone quiescent around them, the after-dinner crowd thinned out, the freezer humming its one low note. By the late twenties the questions had stopped being a game, and the counterpoint she'd felt at the start, the part of her running a commentary, taking notes, grading the date, had gone quiet too. She asked him question thirty-three, the one about what you would change in how you were raised, and he answered it so honestly and at such length that his Midnight Thunder melted entirely down his wrist and he didn't notice until he gestured with that hand and flicked ice cream onto the window.

They were both laughing, the loud kind, the kind the teenage employee behind the counter glances over at, when Nicole realized they had reached thirty-five. He had never used his skip.

"Last one," she said. "You sure you don't want the skip now? Final offer."

Elijah looked at the melted wreckage of his cone, then at her, and folded the napkin into a small square with great ceremony. "Give me the question first. I'll decide after."

She read it off her phone, the last of the thirty-six, and set the phone face down on the table so it couldn't watch. The table wobbled once, on its own, as if settling in for the answer.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: Electricity is billed by the kilowatt-hour, so using 600 kilowatt-hours at 15 cents each costs 90 dollars, before any fixed monthly charges.
story:
Nathaniel spread the two leases across the workbench in the garage, weighting the corners with a socket set and a coffee can full of screws. Manuel stood on one side of him, Jasper on the other, and above them the single bulb swung whenever anyone bumped the bench.

"The one on Delgado is four-fifty a month," Manuel said, tapping the page. "The one on Fairview is four-ninety. So it's obvious."

"It's not obvious," Nathaniel said. "Delgado doesn't include utilities. Fairview includes water and trash but not electricity. And there's a fifteen-dollar trash fee at Delgado that's printed on the third page, in a font size I don't want to talk about."

Jasper had the phone, because Jasper was the one willing to call strangers. He had already called the Delgado landlord's office twice that afternoon, and now he dialed a third time while Nathaniel held the second lease flat under the light. "Hi, yes, I called earlier about unit two. My friend wants to know about the electric bill. Like, what did the last tenant actually pay." He paused, covering the receiver. "She's asking if we mean per month."

"Per month," Nathaniel said. "Average. Ask her what the usage was, in kilowatt-hours, and what the rate is."

Jasper repeated it. Then he wrote a number on the margin of the lease with a carpenter's pencil he'd pulled from Ms. Halvorsen's pegboard. When he hung up he said, "She says the last tenant used around six hundred kilowatt-hours a month, and the rate is fifteen cents per kilowatt-hour."

Nathaniel took the pencil and worked it on the back of a parts invoice. Six hundred at fifteen cents each came to ninety dollars, and that was before any fixed monthly charges, which the landlord had mentioned existed but hadn't specified, which Nathaniel wrote at the bottom of the page and underlined twice. "So electricity's at least ninety on top of the rent," he said. "Probably more."

Manuel leaned over the invoice. "So Delgado is four-fifty plus ninety plus fifteen for trash. That's five fifty-five, and Fairview is four-ninety."

"Plus electricity at Fairview," Nathaniel said. "Which we don't know, because the Fairview landlord wouldn't give us a number. She said it 'depends on lifestyle.'"

"Everything depends on lifestyle," Manuel said. "That's phenomenology. I'm taking it as an elective. It means you can't separate the thing from how you experience the thing, so her electric bill is part of her life and yours is part of yours, and they're different." He said this with the confidence of someone four days into a syllabus, and Jasper told him to stop.

They separated the fixed costs from the ones that would move. Rent was fixed, trash was fixed, water was fixed at Fairview, and electricity was the one variable, and Nathaniel drew a line down the invoice and put everything known on the left and everything unknown on the right. The right side was shorter but heavier. He couldn't have said why a shorter list felt heavier, and he didn't try to.

"Here's what I actually think," he said. "If Fairview's electric usage is anywhere near six hundred kilowatt-hours, the two places cost almost the same, and Delgado wins because I know its number. But if Fairview is cheaper to run, if it's smaller, if the windows aren't garbage, then Fairview wins, and I can't know that from a lease. I'd have to go stand in the room."

Manuel had spent the whole week vilifying the Fairview landlord on the grounds of the small font alone, and now he crossed his arms. "So you're picking Delgado."

"I'm picking knowing things over not knowing things," Nathaniel said. "Which isn't the same as picking Delgado."

Jasper was already dialing again. "I'm going to ask the Fairview office if they'll tell us the last tenant's usage. It worked once." He stepped out through the side door into the driveway, and through the gap Nathaniel could see him pacing on the concrete with the pencil still behind his ear. Manuel picked up the Delgado lease and read the small print on the third page again, mouthing the words. Somewhere in the garage a compressor cycled on, and the bulb swung, and the two leases slid a quarter inch toward each other across the bench.

When Jasper came back in, he held up the invoice paper. On it he'd written a single figure, and nothing else.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: In 1902, French colonial authorities in Hanoi paid a bounty for each rat tail, and people began cutting off tails and releasing the rats to breed, so the rat problem grew.
story:
Keira would like it recorded that she was completely calm during the quarterfinal, though Meghan later said her hands were shaking so hard the notecards sounded like applause. The resolution was "This house believes financial incentives improve moral behavior," and Keira had drawn affirmative, which she had not wanted and had told no one she had not wanted, because a debater who admits her side feels wrong is already losing.

The room smelled like radiator dust and someone's vanilla latte. Ms. Petrov sat at the judge's table with her glasses pushed up into her hair, which she only did when she was interested. Ziyad opened for the negative, and he was good, the kind of good that mesmerized the back row into stillness. "Every incentive," he said, "is a message about what we think people are. Pay a child to read and you tell her reading is a chore. The crowding out of intrinsic motivation is well documented." Keira wrote crowding out and underlined it twice, though later she could not remember why she had underlined it, or whether she had invented the tremor in his voice that made her certain he was bluffing.

Her grandfather's dinner table was where she had first heard about the rats, though for two years she had believed it happened in Paris. Her mother had corrected her at Thanksgiving, gently, the way you correct someone's pronunciation. "Hanoi," her mother said. "Nineteen oh two. The French colonial authorities paid a bounty for each rat tail, and people began cutting off the tails and releasing the rats to breed, so the rat problem grew." Keira had been sixteen and mostly watching her phone, but the image had stuck: a small pile of tails on a clerk's desk, somewhere behind them a city filling up with tailless rats.

So when she stood for her rebuttal, she did the thing that felt like a trap and a door at once. "My opponent is right that incentives can backfire," she said. "In 1902, French colonial authorities in Hanoi paid a bounty for each rat tail, and people began cutting off the tails and releasing the rats to breed, so the rat problem grew." She let it sit. "But notice what that example actually shows. It shows an incentive that rewarded the wrong proxy. A tail is not a dead rat. The lesson isn't that incentives corrupt; it's that we have a responsibility to measure what we actually want. Trade-offs are real, and unintended consequences are real, and the answer to both is better design, not abandonment."

Ziyad's cross-examination was where it went strange. "You concede my whole case," he said. "You just described an unintended consequence and called it a design flaw." "I said consequences are foreseeable if you think hard enough," she said, and heard, as she said it, that this was more faith than she had. The fifty-fifty split in her chest, the equivocal feeling she'd carried since the coin toss, did not go away because she had made a good argument. She was arguing that systems could be engineered toward virtue while privately suspecting that people were not so programmable, and the room could probably see both.

Ms. Petrov's question in the feedback period was short. "Ms. Keira, is there any incentive you personally would refuse on principle, even a well-designed one?" Keira opened her mouth. What came out was "I'd want to see the evidence first," which was not an answer, and everyone knew it, and Meghan put her face in her hands two rows back. But underneath the embarrassment Keira noticed something else: she had refused to lie, and the refusal had cost her, and that was itself a kind of evidence for her side that she could not enter into the record.

They lost on a 2-1 decision. Ziyad was gracious in the hallway, offering her half his protein bar, saying her rat story would show up in his own cases for the next four years. "Steal it," she said. "It's my mother's anyway." He laughed, and she let him believe she was joking, because the truth, that a story about colonial bureaucrats and tails had been passed to her like an heirloom at a table with gravy on it, seemed too tender to explain in a hallway that smelled like bleacher sponge.

Walking out, Meghan asked if she was devastated. Keira said it was not the worst loss, which was litotes and also a lie, and Meghan, who knew her, said, "So you're devastated." The evening was cold for April. In the parking lot Keira found the notecard with crowding out on it, creased down the middle, and she stood between the light poles holding it, deciding whether to throw it away or keep it for the semifinal next year, which neither of them had qualified for.

"Keep it," Meghan said from the car, leaning across to push the door open. Keira folded it once more and put it in her pocket.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The Maillard reaction, between amino acids and sugars, browns food and creates much of its flavor; it proceeds rapidly at about 140 to 165 degrees Celsius.
story:
Aaron had promised his mother a proper dinner on Friday, the night her shift ended at nine, because lately she came home too tired to cook and too proud to say so. He had made chicken, the way he always made it, in the steamer basket with the lid clamped down, and it came out pale and rubbery, sweating on the plate. His grandfather ate it without complaint, but he ate everything without complaint, which was its own kind of honesty. His mother smiled at him across the table, and that smile was worse than criticism, because it meant she was protecting him from something he had done.

The following Tuesday he stood in Ms. Perera's cooking classroom at the long steel counters, chopping an onion badly, and told Aidan about it. Aidan was browning beef for the class stew, and the smell of it kept drifting over, dark and savoury, nothing like Aaron's chicken. "Your pan wasn't hot enough," Aidan said, not looking up. "Mine either, first time."

Ms. Perera moved between the counters in her canvas apron, tasting, correcting, refusing to valorize any single technique over another. "Brown food tastes different," she said only, when Aaron asked her about it, and passed on toward the ovens, because she believed, Aaron had learned, in letting students ruin things first. He found this philosophy admirable in general and useless in the moment.

That night Aidan sent him a message, and Aaron sat on his bed and read it twice.

"ok so i looked it up. its called the Maillard reaction. amino acids and sugars, when the food is hot enough, and it browns the food and makes most of the flavor. it goes fast at about 140 to 165 celsius. your steamer never got near that. pan has to be hot before the chicken goes in. dont crowd it either. seriously dont crowd it"

Below that, a second message: "also audrey-anne says she'll bring dessert friday if you dont burn the house down"

Aaron read the numbers again. He understood, in a vague way, that his chicken had failed not because he was careless but because it had never been given the one thing it needed. He thought of his English class, where they had spent a week on how a part can stand for a whole, the crown for the king, the pen for the writer. His mother called his grandfather's whole philosophy of eating "waste not," and he saw now that the phrase was the same trick, two words standing in for an entire childhood of rationing and rice. In that class Ms. Perera would have been called parochial, maybe, for acting as if her way of cooking was the only way, except that she never had, and neither, he realized, had his grandfather, who ate pale chicken without a word.

On Friday he came home early and set the pan on the burner and waited, longer than felt reasonable, until a drop of water skated across the surface and vanished. He laid the chicken in skin-side down and it shouted at him, a hard hiss, and he flinched and then didn't. The edges went gold, then amber, then a brown he had never produced in his life. He turned the pieces only once, the way the message said, and did not crowd the pan, working in two batches even though it took longer, because his mother's bus came at nine and there was time. Audrey-Anne arrived at eight with a lemon tart she had made in her own kitchen, carrying it flat like something rescued from a fire, and she and the grandfather sat at the table while Aaron cooked, and the whole apartment began to smell like a place where something good was happening.

When his mother came through the door, she stopped in the hallway with her coat still on. "What is that," she said, which was not really a question, and she sat down before she had fully decided to. The skin crackled under her fork. She ate one piece slowly, then a second one faster, and the grandfather took seconds too, and Audrey-Anne, who had been nervous about the tart, watched everyone try it and then relaxed enough to have some herself.

"Since when do you cook like this?" his mother asked.

"Since Tuesday," Aaron said, and he thought about telling her the whole chain of it, the failed chicken, the stew, the message on his phone, the numbers, the pan shouting when the heat was right. There were still things he did not know, like why the second batch browned unevenly at the edges, and whether he could do it again tomorrow, or whether it had been partly luck. He decided to say only part of it, the part that was finished. "Aidan helped."

"Aidan gets the leftovers," his mother said, already reaching for the plate.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: In his 1961 book Griff nach der Weltmacht, German historian Fritz Fischer argued that Imperial Germany deliberately pursued a world war, setting off a long debate known as the Fischer controversy.
story:
Hannah found the plaque in the war gallery before she found Abbey, which was the usual order of things. It hung beside a photograph of men in coal-scuttle helmets, and it said something careful and vague about "the complex origins of the conflict." She copied the phrase into her phone, because her textbook at home said something different, and the textbook Loucas had photographed from his cousin's school said something different again, and the essay was due on Monday.

"There you are," Abbey said, arriving with two postcards, one of which she handed over without comment. It showed a cavalry horse in a gas mask. "Loucas is buying a pen he doesn't need. He wants to argue with you about the war."

"He can remonstrate all he likes," Hannah said. "I'm just trying to find out what actually happened." The word had come from her mother, who used it whenever the neighbours put their bins out early, and it felt right here too, the idea of a formal objection, lodged on the record.

Loucas caught up with them at the case of medals, holding his pen like evidence. "My book says Germany bears the main responsibility. Yours spreads it around. They can't both be right."

"Maybe they were written before different things were known," Abbey said, tilting her head at the cavalry postcard.

Ms. Chanthavong, who taught at their school and had, for reasons no one had dared ask, come to the museum on the same Saturday, appeared beside the photograph of the helmets. She did not explain anything. She said only, "There's a display in the next room you two should read," and moved on toward an elderly man struggling with the map of the floor plan, whom she began helping with the patient air of someone who had done it before.

The display was a wall of historians' books, and Hannah read the caption twice. In his 1961 book Griff nach der Weltmacht, the German historian Fritz Fischer had argued that Imperial Germany deliberately pursued a world war, and the claim had set off a long debate that had its own name, the Fischer controversy. She said the name aloud to hear it. "The Fischer controversy," she said. "That's a thing people call it."

"It sounds like a scandal," Loucas said.

"It kind of was. People were furious with him. Other historians said he was wrong." She stood back from the wall. The subtlety of it was beginning to reach her: it was not that one book was true and the other false, but that a question had been asked in 1961 that had not been asked the same way before, and once asked, it would not go away. Her textbook was older than the argument in some ways and younger in others; Loucas's book had absorbed part of the fight and not the rest. The sources everyone drew on were the same yellowed telegrams, and the telegrams had not changed, but the people reading them had.

She remembered, suddenly, being eleven and asking her grandmother which of her two brothers had started the fight that broke the porch swing, and her grandmother saying, "Which time?" There had been no single fight. There had been years of them, and the swing was just where the years had finally given way. Hannah had thought it was a non-answer then. She thought now it might have been the most perspicacious thing anyone had ever told her, an answer that saw through the question to what the question was leaving out.

"I still have to write the essay," she said. "Monday. One page, who caused it."

"So pick one," Loucas said.

"I don't think I can pick one and be honest." She looked at the wall of books again, at the spines in their different decades. "Maybe I write about why the books disagree. Maybe that's the actual answer, or the closest thing to one."

Abbey, who had been quiet, held out her phone. On the screen was a photo she had taken of the two of them in front of the medals case, mid-argument, both of them pointing at the glass. "For when you're famous," she said.

Ms. Chanthavong passed them again on her way out, the elderly man now equipped with a map and a folded reading chair voucher. She paused at Hannah's notebook, saw the copied phrase and the name underlined twice, and said nothing, but the corner of her mouth moved.

Loucas bought a second pen at the shop, because the first one was for his sister. At the door, Hannah stopped and looked back down the gallery toward the photograph of the helmets.

"Grandmother would have liked this place," she said.

"Did she fight in the war?" Loucas asked.

"No. She just never believed in one cause for anything."

Outside, Abbey took her arm, and they started down the steps toward the bus stop, the essay still unwritten and the notebook warm in Hannah's bag.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: On Mexico's Day of the Dead, orange marigolds called cempasúchil decorate altars and graves, because their bright color and strong scent are thought to guide the souls of the dead home.
story:
The marigolds were the wrong color, and Jaxon knew it before he reached the cemetery gate. He had bought them at the grocery store that morning because the flower stall on Fifth Street was closed, and they were pale, almost yellow, the kind of orange that had given up halfway. His grandmother had died in September, three weeks into his first semester, and he had missed enough classes already that his professor had sent him a note asking, in an incisive little sentence, whether he intended to finish the course. He intended to finish it. He also intended to do this right, whatever right meant, and he was not sure the two intentions fit in the same day.

Emmanuelle was waiting for him at the gate with a paper bag from the panadería and a look that meant she had opinions. "Those are sad," she said. "Those are groceries."

"They're marigolds," Jaxon said. "Botanically, they're marigolds."

"Botanically." She said the word like he had failed a test she hadn't told him about. "Your abuela did the altar every year. I saw it once, when I stayed for dinner. It was like a fire in the front room. Those are not a fire."

Inside, the cemetery was doing its October business: leaves gathering against headstones, a maintenance man raking the same patch of grass he had probably raken that morning, a crow sitting on the oldest monument as if it were a savant of something, patient and unimpressed. Jaxon's grandmother had a plot near the fence line, under a maple that Reese, who came to funerals the way other people came to parties, had described as "objectively beautiful." Reese wasn't here today. Reese had a midterm. Emmanuelle had skipped something, and had not said what, and Jaxon had decided not to ask.

He set the pale marigolds on the grass and stood there with his hands in his pockets. At home, in his grandmother's kitchen, there was a shoebox he had not opened yet, and inside it, folded into quarters, a letter she had written him the summer before, which his mother had found while clearing the apartment and passed along with the words, she wanted you to have this while you were at school. He had read it twice on the bus. Certain parts of it he could recite. When you are young you will malign the slow days, she had written, because you cannot yet see that the slow days are the ones you get to keep. He had looked up malign on his phone, feeling stupid about it, and then feeling worse, because she had used it exactly right.

"Say it out loud," Emmanuelle said now. She had sat down cross-legged on the grass without asking, as though the plot were a living room. "Whatever you were going to say. You've been rehearsing it since the gate, I can tell, your mouth does a thing."

"My mouth does not do a thing."

"Your mouth does a thing."

He exhaled. "In Spanish they have a name for them. The real ones. Cempasúchil. She said it once, in her kitchen, when I asked why she bought so many, why not roses, why not anything else. She said on the Day of the Dead people put them on the altars and the graves because they're so bright and they smell so strong that the dead can follow them home. The souls. They follow the color and the smell, like a road." He looked down at the flowers he had brought, their washed-out heads, their grocery-store nothing scent. "So you see the problem."

"The problem is you brought the dead a road made of beige."

"Thank you. Yes. That's the problem."

Emmanuelle opened her paper bag, took out one pan dulce, broke it in half, and set half of it on the edge of the plot, crumbs and all. "My dad does this," she said. "He's not even that superstitious. He just says you don't show up to somebody's house without bringing something, and you don't leave the house without leaving something behind." She brushed sugar off her fingers. "There's a mercado on Saturdays. The one in the church basement, the little one. The abuelas sell flowers out of buckets. If you go early enough, before ten, they have the real ones, the orange ones, the ones that smell like the whole thing is true."

"It's Thursday."

"So you come back Saturday. You bring the real ones, and these ones stay here until then, as a, I don't know, as a placeholder." She said placeholder carefully, like a word she was testing for weight. "Or you don't come back, and it's flowers, and she knows you came, and maybe that's the whole of it anyway."

Jaxon thought about his philosophy seminar, where the professor had spent two weeks on the question of whether a symbol had to work in order to mean anything, whether a ritual that failed was still a ritual. He had written an essay arguing that intent carried the meaning. He had gotten an A-minus and a comment in the margin: consider the counterargument. He was considering it now, standing over the wrong flowers, the intent standing there with him and getting him nothing.

He picked up the grocery-store marigolds, held them a moment, then set them back down, rearranged so their best faces turned outward toward the path. The crow on the old monument shifted its weight and did not leave. Emmanuelle tore the pan dulce into smaller pieces and lined them along the headstone, and Jaxon took out his phone and typed himself a reminder, Saturday, before ten, church basement, and under it, after a pause, a second line: ask the abuela which bucket. He put the phone away and knelt and pulled one weed from the base of the stone, then another, working slowly while the light went long and gold across the grass.

"So Saturday," Emmanuelle said from the grass beside him, "you're buying, and I'm carrying."

"Deal," Jaxon said, and reached for the next weed.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Cindy Sherman's Untitled Film Stills (1977 to 1980) is a series of 70 black-and-white photographs of herself posed as characters from imaginary movies.
story:
Alexis had taped ten sheets of printer paper above his desk like a detective's conspiracy board, except the conspiracy was him. Every sheet said SELF in his handwriting, then a small variation: SELF IN MIRROR, SELF AT BUS STOP, SELF AS VILLAIN. He sat on his bed with a sketchbook and a peanut butter sandwich, glaring at the wall as though it were holding something back.

The problem had arrived two weeks earlier, when Mr. Wong had announced the portfolio assignment in the art room that smelled faintly of turpentine and oranges. Ten artworks, one theme, plus an artist's statement, which Mr. Wong had described as "one page that tells us what your eyes were doing." Alexis had raised his hand and asked if the theme could be himself, and Mr. Wong had said, "It can, if you can keep ten pictures of your own face from becoming one picture repeated ten times." The class had laughed, kindly, and Alexis had laughed too, and then had gone home and not solved it at all.

His sketches so far were, honestly, identical. Same jaw, same worried eyebrows, same attempt at a mysterious gaze that looked more like a boy trying to remember if he'd locked the front door. His mother had leaned in on her way past with laundry and said, "Nice. Very symmetrical," which was not the review he was after.

He texted Kaitlyn, who answered at eleven at night because she kept worse hours than he did. "come over tomorrow," she wrote. "i have a REVELATION. bring snacks." Danae was added to the thread without consultation, as was tradition.

Saturday afternoon, the three of them sat on his bedroom floor around the sandwich remains and a bag of pretzels Kaitlyn had brought as her contribution to scholarship. She produced her phone with ceremony, holding it face down like a card she was deciding whether to play. "Okay. So. I was doom-scrolling instead of writing my history essay, and I found this photographer. Cindy Sherman. She did a whole series, Untitled Film Stills, from 1977 to 1980, and get this." She flipped the phone over. "Seventy photographs. All black and white. All of herself."

"Seventy," Alexis repeated, chewing.

"Posed as characters from imaginary movies. Movies that don't exist. She's like a secretary in one and a runaway in another and a housewife who looks like she's about to commit a crime with a frying pan." Kaitlyn scrolled, and there they were: grainy, dramatic, a woman becoming different women while remaining, unmistakably, the same woman.

Danae leaned over Alexis's shoulder. "So it's still her face the whole time?"

"That's the whole point," Kaitlyn said. "It's her, but it's also not."

Alexis looked at the little screen, then at his wall of doomed SELF sheets, and felt something rearrange itself behind his ribs. He got up, pulled the sheet down that said SELF AS VILLAIN, and turned it over. On the back he wrote, in letters too big for the paper, characters from movies that were never made.

"This is either genius or plagiarism," Danae said.

"It's neither, it's an homage," Alexis said. "There's a difference. Probably."

For the next three hours the room became something between a studio and a low-budget film set. Danae found his mother's old scarf and draped it over his head like a doomed heroine from a black-and-white movie about a woman on a train. Kaitlyn, directing with the gravity of someone who had read half an article about cinematography, positioned his desk lamp low and to the side and said, "The light should presage doom. Like something bad is about to happen but politely." Alexis did not ask her where she'd learned the word; she used words like that the way other people used gum, constantly and with visible satisfaction. He held a watering can as though it were evidence in a murder and let her take the picture on his phone in black and white.

They did nine more setups before his mother knocked to ask why the laundry basket was on his head. He explained that he was a fugitive in an imagined film of unresolved genre, and she said, "As long as the laundry gets folded, fugitive," and went downstairs, which Alexis felt was reasonably supportive.

Later, alone, he sat at his desk with the ten photographs open on his laptop in a grid. He was himself in all of them and also, somehow, ten other people: a waiter, a witness, a man at a bus stop at midnight in a story no one had filmed. He began drafting the artist's statement, deleted his first sentence because it sounded bombastic, something about "the fracturing of identity in the modern gaze," and wrote instead, "I wanted to know if a face could lie on purpose." He chewed his pen. It could, he thought, but he wasn't sure yet whether the lie told the truth or just replaced it, and he suspected Mr. Wong would ask exactly that.

He printed the statement, taped it to the center of the wall, and stood back next to the last self, the boy holding a watering can like a verdict.

"I'm going with it," he said, to nobody, to all of them.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, describing how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it.
story:
Victoria had mixed the same gray four times, and it still refused to behave. On the left side of her canvas, where it lapped against the orange of the brick warehouse, the gray looked almost lavender; on the right, against the blue tarp of the fish stall, the very same paint went cool and steely, like wet slate. She held her brush above the board and did not move it. Around her the community studio clattered with the Tuesday evening crowd: a retired man varnishing a spoon collection, two kids finger-painting a dinosaur apocalypse, and Rachel, who was supposed to be drawing her own still life but was mostly texting.

"Stop staring at your sky," Rachel said without looking up. "It's creepy."

"It's broken." Victoria turned the canvas toward her. "Same gray, two sides, two colors. Tell me I'm not hallucinating."

Rachel squinted, then tilted her head, then picked up the canvas and carried it under the skylight, as if better light might shame the paint into consistency. It did not. "Okay, that's genuinely weird. Ask Mr. Gauthier."

Mr. Gauthier ran the studio on Tuesdays and Thursdays, a heavyset man in a cardigan with a hole in the elbow, famous among the regulars for his scathing critiques of anyone who traced. Victoria, who had been coming for only six weeks, was still enough of a neophyte to be frightened of him. She carried the canvas over anyway, because the alternative was repainting the sky for a fifth time.

He looked for a long moment. Then, instead of explaining, he went to the shelf of donated books and set a fat, spine-cracked volume in front of her. "Look up Chevreul," he said, and wandered off to stop the younger kids from varnishing the dinosaur.

The book was from 1839, the printed date on the title page, a translation of something by a chemist named Michel Eugène Chevreul. Victoria ran her finger down the table of contents until she found it: the law of simultaneous contrast. She read the page twice. A color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it. She sat back on the stool. The orange bricks, the blue tarp. The gray hadn't changed at all; her eyes had. It was like learning that a magician's trick was a mirror the whole time, and finding the mirror more interesting than the dove.

"Find anything?" Rachel had drifted over.

"It's called the law of simultaneous contrast," Victoria said, tapping the page. "This chemist, Chevreul, published it in 1839. A color shifts toward the complement of whatever's next to it. So my gray leans purple next to orange and cool next to blue. My sky isn't broken. It's doing exactly what it's supposed to."

"That's infuriating," Rachel said. "So you can't paint the color you actually mixed?"

Victoria looked at the canvas for a while. She could fight it, she supposed, and nudge the left gray one way and the right gray the other, forcing them to match, and the sky would read flat and dead, a gray that had been argued into submission. Or she could let the effect work, which felt less like painting and more like negotiating with her own eyes. It bothered her that she couldn't fully predict it, that she would have to look, and adjust, and look again, and that even then she'd be guessing at what another person would see standing three feet back. She'd wanted the sky to be one thing. It was going to be at least two.

She mixed a fresh batch, slightly warmer than her reference, and laid it in along the bricks. Standing back, she judged it close, though close to what, exactly, she could no longer say with certainty, and decided she could live with that.

Mr. Gauthier drifted past on his way to the kiln and paused. "Better," he said, which from him was practically a parade.

"Don't valorize me," Victoria said, testing the word she'd found in the book's introduction, where the translator complained that optical studies had been unfairly ignored.

"I said better, not good." He moved on. Rachel laughed so hard she smudged her still life, and then complained about it for ten minutes, and the studio closed at nine with the sky still undecided, and Victoria carried it out under the streetlights, where it looked, briefly, like a third color entirely.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The notation dy/dx for a derivative comes from Gottfried Leibniz and is still standard in mathematics today.
story:
The community centre smelled of chlorine and floor wax, and the math table by the vending machines had a wobble that Anais had learned to brace with her knee. She spread her notebook flat, smoothed the page, and copied the problem from the whiteboard Mr. Do had left standing from the afternoon class: a polynomial, and beneath it, in his looping hand, the words "find the maximum."

"You're doing this voluntarily," said Finley, dropping into the chair opposite with a bag of chips. "On a Thursday. In July."

"The scholarship exam is Tuesday." Anais sharpened her pencil over the bin, watching the shavings fall. "If I place into calculus, they pay for the whole first year." She did not add what the guidance counsellor had said, that the exam was graded on a curve against everyone else sitting it, including the boy from the magnet school whose practice scores were already a small legend. She didn't say his name either, though Kellan had said it twice last week, casually, watching her face both times.

Mr. Do came back with two teas and sat down without ceremony. "So. Yesterday you learned the rule. Today you learn what the rule is for." He wrote y equals x cubed minus six x squared plus nine x, then drew a wavy curve beneath it like a hill. "The derivative tells you the slope at every point. Where does a hilltop live, in terms of slope?"

"Where the slope is zero," Anais said, and he nodded and left her to it, which was his way, and which she had learned to prefer to being told.

She worked the derivative term by term, lips moving. Three x squared minus twelve x plus nine. Set it equal to zero. Factor. x equals one, x equals three. The curve rose to one, sank, rose again to three, and only one of them was a peak. She checked the slope just before and just after three, saw it swing from negative to positive, and felt something click into place like a lock that had only been waiting for the right key.

"It's a fraction," Finley said, reading over her shoulder. He pointed at the notation on the formula sheet, dy over dx. "Why does the textbook write it like a fraction if it isn't one?"

"Blame Leibniz," Mr. Do said, sipping his tea. "That notation is his, and it's still what everyone uses." He would say nothing further; Anais had tried to draw him out before and he only smiled into his cup. So she looked it up herself on the centre's ancient computer while Finley remonstrated with the vending machine, which had taken his dollar and given him nothing, and she found that the odd little d's had survived three hundred years, outliving rival notations the way a dialect outlives an empire. Something written as a lie that worked better than the truth. She wrote that in the margin, then crossed it out because it wasn't math.

The envelope was waiting when she got home. She had applied weeks ago and forgotten, in the way you forget things you want too much, and here it was, thin, from the cosmopolitan arts program she'd abandoned in her head last spring when the money question killed it. Inside was a single page: the program had a seat for her, tuition covered, if she confirmed by August. Not the scholarship. A different life, parallel to this one, both of them suddenly real at once. Her mother read it over her shoulder and said nothing, which said everything, and Anais folded it into her textbook between chapters seven and eight, where the derivative lived.

Kellan texted at ten: "heard you're sitting the calc exam. so am I." Then: "one of us gets the top mark and the interview. no hard feelings either way?" She stared at the screen for a long time, the cursor blinking, and typed and deleted three replies before settling on "no hard feelings." She meant it about half, which was as honest as the phone allowed. What she did not type was that the envelope had changed the arithmetic, that there were now two maximums on her curve and she could only stand on one.

Tuesday came the way exam days come, too fast and then too slow. She sat three rows behind Kellan and watched the back of his head, his cowlick, his easy shoulders, and resented and liked him in the same breath. The polynomial on the exam was nastier than Mr. Do's, a fourth degree thing with ugly coefficients, but she took its derivative, set it to zero, factored until her fingers ached, and found the peak sitting between two numbers like a bird on a wire. She wrote dy/dx at the top of her solution, the old borrowed fraction, and underlined it, and had a moment of absurd tenderness for a dead man she'd never meet.

The results would come by post, the old-fashioned denouement, and the envelope from the arts program sat in her drawer with six days left to answer. On Thursday she was back at the wobbly table, this time teaching Finley the power rule while he ate his chips and got it wrong twice and then, gloriously, right. Mr. Do collected the empty tea cups. "You never told me," he said, "which way you're going."

Anais looked at the hill she had drawn in Finley's notebook, its little peak flagged with an arrow, and then out the window at the summer light going long and amber over the parking lot. "I told them yes," she said. "And I'm sitting the interview anyway."

"Both?"

"Both," she said, and picked up her pencil.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: According to the CDC, US drivers aged 16 to 19 have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged 20 and older, per mile driven.
story:
Eric sat in the driver's seat of Mr. Lawson's Buick with his hands at ten and two, the way the pamphlet showed, and listened to the engine idle in his own driveway. His mother stood on the porch with her coffee, not waving, not coming closer, and he understood that her staying there was its own kind of permission. Mr. Lawson settled into the passenger seat with a grunt and dropped a set of keys into the cupholder as if they were nothing, though Eric had watched him wipe the dashboard down before they started, twice.

"You checked the mirrors," Mr. Lawson said. It wasn't a question. "Good. Now tell me what you're going to do before you do it, out loud, until it's boring."

"Put it in reverse. Back down the driveway to the street." The words felt clumsy, like narrating himself from the outside, but he said them anyway, and when the car rolled backward under his own foot, slow as syrup, something in his chest went strange. He had waited two years past his birthday for this. Part of the delay had been money, part of it had been his mother's silence on the subject, and part of it, which he was only now admitting, had been him.

Lydia had told him the number last spring, standing in the parking lot after school with her permit still warm in her pocket. She'd read it off a poster at the licensing office while she waited for her test, some CDC statistic, and she'd recited it to him almost cheerfully, the way she delivered everything. Drivers sixteen to nineteen, she said, have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers twenty and older, per mile driven. Almost three times. Per mile. She'd shrugged afterward and said her mom called the poster a scare tactic, and then Camron had leaned out his window and honked, and the whole conversation had scattered like birds.

He had let it scatter. That was the past choice he kept turning over now, easing the Buick down his street at fifteen miles an hour while Mr. Lawson murmured about stopping distances. He'd decided, back then, that the statistic was about other kids, kids like Camron who treated the interstate like a proving ground. Eric was careful. Eric checked mirrors. The fact had sat in him for a year without doing any work, the way a vestigial thing sits in a body, carried along but unused.

"Stop sign," Mr. Lawson said, and Eric stopped, a full beat longer than he needed to, and checked both ways twice. Mr. Lawson made a small sound that might have been approval. "You know," he said, "my wife wanted me to sell this car after Danny left for college. I told her he'd need something to come home to."

"Where'd he go?" Eric asked, glad for the talk, glad for anything to hold onto while he turned left onto the wider road.

"Georgia. Three years ago." Mr. Lawson's voice went flat in a way Eric recognized from his own mother. He did not ask the next question, but Mr. Lawson answered it anyway, looking out at the hedges going by. "Not a car thing. Don't worry, it's not a car thing. Leukemia, when he was fifteen." A pause. "He never even got to fail a driving test like a normal kid."

They drove on. The road opened past the elementary school, and Eric felt the steering loosen under his hands, the car wanting speed, wanting the freedom everyone kept promising him it carried. He had believed in that promise the way Lydia believed in her parking lot statistics, lightly, certain it applied to strangers. But the two ideas had been sitting side by side in him all this time, the emancipation and the danger, and only now, with his foot actually on the pedal, did he see they were both true at once and neither cancelled the other out.

"Can I ask you something?" Eric said. "Why'd you offer to teach me? Mom said you don't even talk to the neighbors."

Mr. Lawson was quiet long enough that Eric checked the mirror just to have somewhere to look. "Because I watched you not drive," he said finally. "Two years. You'd stand at the end of the driveway when the school bus came, and I could never tell if you were waiting for it or dreading it. A person who hesitates that long is either a coward or paying attention. I figured I'd find out which."

Eric held the wheel steady through the next turn. He didn't have an answer for that yet, and he was tired of pretending he did. Maybe the statistic was a scare tactic and maybe it was just arithmetic, and maybe the honest thing was to hold both, to drive carefully not because he was afraid but because he had chosen to notice what fear was for. He signaled, checked the mirror, and pulled back onto his own street, where his mother was still on the porch, coffee gone cold in her hands.

"Again tomorrow?" Mr. Lawson asked as Eric shut off the engine in the driveway, clean, precise, no curb kissed.

"Yeah," Eric said. "Same time." And up on the porch, for the first time all morning, his mother lifted her cup toward the windshield.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Canada lowered its federal voting age from 21 to 18 in 1970.
story:
The line outside the community hall moved in short, patient shuffles, and Aiden checked his voter card for the third time, though the information on it had not changed. Today was the first election he had ever been old enough to vote in, having turned eighteen in March, and he was surprised by how ceremonial it felt to stand in a school gymnasium that smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee. His father had dropped him off with a wave and a single comment: "Knock yourself out." Aiden knew what that meant. His father believed elections were theatre, that the real decisions were made somewhere the ballots never reached, and he said so every time the subject arose, usually while the news droned in the kitchen. Aiden had absorbed enough of that view to be embarrassed by his own nervousness, and enough of the opposite view, from Adeline, who had phone-banked for weeks, to feel ashamed of the embarrassment.

Adeline was already inside, standing near the registration table with Anais, who was seventeen and therefore stuck on the wrong side of the age line for another eight months. "You're actually doing it," Anais said when she saw him. "Our first voter. Historically speaking." She had a habit of framing small events as history, and usually he teased her for it, but today it landed differently, made the cardboard voting screens, arranged across the gym floor like an archipelago of flimsy islands, seem like something with a past attached.

"How long have eighteen-year-olds even been allowed to do this?" Aiden asked, partly to fill the silence, partly because the question had genuinely been circling him all morning. "It feels like something people fought for."

"It has to be ages," Anais said. "Like, at least a hundred years. People our age got the vote after some huge fight, like women did."

Aiden nodded, because that matched his vague sense of things, and Adeline pulled out her phone. "Hold on, I'm not repeating a fact I haven't checked," she said, thumbs already moving. She was constitutionally incapable of repeating a fact she hadn't checked, which was annoying at parties and useful everywhere else. "Canada lowered the federal voting age from twenty-one to eighteen in 1970," she read. "Nineteen seventy. That's it."

"Seventy?" Anais said. "That's basically yesterday. My parents were alive."

"Your parents were alive and still couldn't vote at your age," Adeline said. "Which is a strange sentence."

Aiden did the arithmetic in his head and found it disorienting. Not a century of tradition but a single generation and change; young enough that some of the people in this line had turned twenty-one under the old rule and had watched the number drop. He had assumed a long inheritance and instead he was standing inside something recent, provisional, a door that had been unlocked while the building was already standing.

Ms. Vu, who lived three doors down from his family and was working the registration table, called his name as he approached. "Aiden. Grown up and everything." She found him on her list and slid a ballot across to him, and when he fumbled the folder she waited without hurrying him, the way she used to wait at her kitchen table when he was stuck on math homework in grade six. "Take your time in there," she said quietly. "It's not a test."

In the booth, alone with the pencil, he looked at the names and found himself hearing both voices at once, his father's flat certainty that none of it mattered and Adeline's equally flat certainty that it did, and neither voice was entirely his. His father was not wrong about power, he thought; there were forces no ballot could circumscribe, money that moved before campaigns even started. But his father had also stopped believing that anything could be nudged, and Adeline had not stopped, and the fact on Adeline's phone sat in his mind, that the age had come down from twenty-one to eighteen in his parents' lifetime, that someone had decided the circle was drawn too tightly and had redrawn it. Small things did move. He did not know if his ballot was one of them. He made his marks anyway, folded the paper along its creases, and carried it to the box like something breakable.

Outside, Anais was waiting on the steps with two coffees, one held out for him. "So," she said. "Feel powerful?"

"I don't know what I feel yet," Aiden said. "Ask me in four years when you're in there."

"Eight months," Anais said, and clinked her cup against his. Down the block, his father's car idled at the curb, engine running, and Aiden took a long drink and did not move toward it yet.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Freezer burn happens when air dries out the surface of frozen food; it makes food tough and tasteless but does not make it unsafe to eat.
story:
Jackson had agreed to cook for the week at the campsite mostly because his father had said it would be good for him, and because Abbas had said, "You'll poison us," which Jackson took as a challenge.

The plan was his own contrivance, drafted on graph paper in the car: seven dinners, one big shop, three cooking sessions, everything portioned into containers and frozen against the back half of the week. Gwenyth, who was along because her mother and his had arranged it years ago and neither girl nor boy had been consulted since, read the plan over his shoulder and said it looked like a bombing run. He chose to take this as a compliment.

The shop took two hours because Jackson had never bought a whole bag of carrots before, or considered that oil came in sizes, or known that chicken thighs were cheaper than breasts and, according to a handwritten card in the cooler, better for stew. Abbas, stationed at the cart, had become strangely loquacious in the meat aisle, narrating the marbling of each cut like a golf announcer, which slowed things down but kept morale up.

The first cooking session was a stew. Jackson browned the thighs, sweated the onions until Abbas stopped calling them raw, and let the pot sit on the edge of the fire grate for two hours while they swam. It tasted, Gwenyth admitted under pressure, better than acceptable. He portioned it into a container that did not seal as well as he had assumed, pressed it into the cooler with the ice, and felt, briefly, like someone who had his life arranged.

On Thursday it had not gone well at the lake, rain presaging worse rain, and they came back early, hungry and short with each other, and Jackson pulled the container out to find the top layer of stew marked with pale, dry patches, gray-white where the sauce should have been glossy. He held it toward the firelight. "Is this mold," Abbas said, not as a question, more as a sentence he had already accepted.

Jackson turned the container slowly. The patches were dry, not fuzzy, and they sat only where the lid had failed and the air had touched the food. He thought of his grandmother's freezer, the ancient chops at the back with the same bleached look, which she had cooked anyway, and of a line he had read somewhere on his phone at one in the morning, half believing it: freezer burn happens when air dries out the surface of frozen food, and it makes the food tough and tasteless but it does not make it unsafe to eat. He had not planned to need the fact. He had saved it the way you save a receipt.

"Freezer burn," he said. "The air got in and dried it out. It's tough and it'll taste like nothing, but it won't hurt us." Abbas looked at him with the expression of a boy deciding whether his friend was brave or the mechanism of his own death. Gwenyth, who was the hungriest, said, "Then scoop off the top layer and feed the rest to me before he changes his mind."

They ate it at the picnic table under the tarp, rain loud on the plastic, and the stew beneath the pale layer was fine, or fine enough, and the layer itself, which Jackson tried first because it seemed unfair to make Abbas the experiment, was exactly as promised: tough and tasteless, like chewing a rainy dishcloth, but nothing worse. Abbas watched him swallow, waited a full ten seconds, and then served himself.

Afterward Jackson sat by the cooler with the graph paper, revising. He drew a box where the container had gone, wrote "better lid or eat this one first," and considered that the plan had not failed so much as revealed itself: the week could be organized, but only up to the seal. He crossed out Wednesday, moved the chili up, and left a margin blank for whatever he had not thought of yet. Gwenyth leaned over, tapped the blank space, and asked what went there.

"I don't know yet," Jackson said, and folded the paper into his pocket.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Monet showed fifteen paintings from his Haystacks series at the Durand-Ruel gallery in May 1891, and most sold within a month.
story:
Nicole taped the tenth sketch to the classroom window and stepped back until her shoulders touched the radiator. Ten drawings of the stairwell behind the gym, the one with the broken window and the light that changed every hour. Ten variations on the same flight of steps.

"Is that all one staircase?" Haiden came in carrying two coffees and handed her one without asking.

"That's the whole point."

"It looks like you couldn't think of anything else."

She pulled the tape off the corner of one drawing and considered hanging it crooked, just to see. Behind her, Mr. Suzuki was stacking chairs for the end of the day, and Spencer was at the far table pinning up his own portfolio, twelve paintings of parking lots, each one with a different car in the foreground. His artist's statement was already printed and laminated. Nicole had read it at lunch. It used the word "ubiquity" twice.

The assignment was due in nine days. Ten artworks around a single theme, plus a statement of one page. She had the drawings. What she did not have was the statement, because every draft she wrote either sounded like a museum plaque or like an apology. Worse, the show would be juried, and the juror was a woman from the community college who had bought a painting from a student two years ago. Nicole wanted a buyer. She had said so out loud exactly once, to Haiden, who had shrugged and said wanting money from art was normal.

"You should ask about whether people buy sets," Haiden said now, watching Spencer arrange his laminated statement at a slight angle. "Like whether buyers want ten of the same thing or whether they want variety. Spencer's got parking lots, you've got stairs. Somebody's wrong."

"Nobody's wrong."

"Then somebody's boring."

That evening Nicole sat in the school library after it had mostly emptied, with her laptop open to the database Mr. Suzuki had shown them in September. She had typed "series" into the search box, meaning to find something about how painters decided when to stop, and had found a scan of a gallery catalogue instead. Monet showed fifteen paintings from his Haystacks series at the Durand-Ruel gallery in May 1891, and most sold within a month. She read the sentence three times. Fifteen pictures of the same haystacks, in the same field, and most were gone in under thirty days. She wrote the date on a sticky note, then felt circumspect about the sticky note, as if the fact might change on her if she handled it too confidently, and folded it into her pocket instead.

The next morning she found Spencer in the hallway by his locker. "Did you know Monet showed fifteen Haystacks paintings at Durand-Ruel in May 1891, and most of them sold within a month?"

Spencer closed his locker. "So?"

"So people buy sets. The same thing over and over, if the light changes."

"The light changes in parking lots too," Spencer said. "Depending on the time of day. It's in my statement."

She looked at him and understood that the fact cut both ways, which annoyed her. It could aggrandize her stairwell, ten versions of one hour, or it could aggrandize his parking lots, and neither of them could claim it alone. What she wanted was a reason her project was the right one, and the haystacks gave her a reason, not a verdict. That distinction sat uncomfortably all through fourth period.

In the studio that afternoon, she taped her drawings in a row on the long wall, lowest to highest light, and stood in the middle of the room with a legal pad. Mr. Suzuki passed behind her with a box of gesso.

"You've ordered them," he said.

"By time. Monet sold most of his Haystacks in a month, so somebody wanted fifteen of the same field." She said it fast, testing it. "But I don't know if that's why I did it or if I'm using him to make it sound bigger than it is."

Mr. Suzuki set the box down and looked at the row of stairs for a moment. "Write the version that admits both," he said, and went back to the supply closet.

She wrote until the bell. The statement came out shorter than she expected, half a page, ending on the question of whether repetition was attention or laziness, and saying that she had decided it was attention, for the stairwell at least, while the haystacks said it could also be commerce, and she could not tell where the line fell. Haiden read it over her shoulder and tapped the last line.

"That's not a denouement," Haiden said. "Nothing wraps up."

"Good," Nicole said, and pulled the tape roll from her back pocket.

She rehung the seventh drawing, the one taken at 4:40 when the broken window threw a bar of light across the bottom step, three inches to the left, so it sat a little out of line with the others. Haiden tilted a head at it. "That one's crooked."

"I know," she said, and left it.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: The 'file drawer problem', a term coined by psychologist Robert Rosenthal in 1979, describes studies with null results going unpublished, which makes the published record look more positive than the evidence.
story:
Olivier spread the two articles across the small table by the window, weighting the corners with his mug and a saucer of sugar packets. The cafe smelled of burnt milk and lemon cleaner. He had been sitting there for forty minutes, and so far his notebook contained one sentence, which he had crossed out.

The assignment was straightforward on its face: compare two scholarly articles on the same question and write a critical review. Ms. Sok had said the review was not a summary, that it should weigh evidence rather than report it, and that a good review could end without deciding. He had believed her at the time. Now the two articles sat in front of him like two witnesses who disagreed, and he could not tell which one was lying, or whether either was.

The first article, by a team in Rotterdam, reported that school start times pushed later improved attendance by a margin Olivier had underlined twice. The second, from a group in Osaka, found no effect at all, and it said so in the flat tone of people who had expected to find something. Emilie arrived with an iced tea and dropped into the other chair without asking.

"You look like you're at a funeral," she said.

"I'm deciding which one to trust."

"Both," she said, and stole a sugar packet. "That's the whole trick. Ms. Sok said that in October."

"It's not both, though. They can't both be right." He turned the Rotterdam pages toward her, then the Osaka pages, then back again, as though the ordering might change something. Emilie read a few lines of each, sucking loudly through her straw.

"Carolyn did her review on this exact question," she said eventually. "For the midterm. She found like fifteen articles and they all said later start times help. Every single one."

"That settles it, then."

"She got a C minus. Ms. Sok wrote something in the margin. Here, I photographed it because Carolyn was furious." Emilie scrolled her phone and held it out. The comment read, in blue ink, "Fifteen positive results. Ask what the file drawer might contain."

"What's a file drawer?" Olivier said.

"No idea. Carolyn wouldn't ask her." Emilie drained her tea and stood, gathering her bag, because her shift at the pool started in twenty minutes and the bus did not wait for epistemology. She left him with the photograph still open on her phone screen, propped against the sugar.

He typed the phrase into his laptop. The screen at the cafe was small and the wifi slow, so the definition loaded in pieces, the way bad news does. The file drawer problem, a term coined by the psychologist Robert Rosenthal in 1979: studies with null results go unpublished, so the published record looks more positive than the evidence. He read it three times. Then he looked at the Osaka article, the one he had privately been treating as the weaker of the two, the boring one, the one that found nothing.

The cafe's radio moved from weather to traffic, portending nothing except the usual congestion on the bridge, though the announcer said the word "unprecedented" anyway. Olivier wrote a new sentence in his notebook. Then he crossed out half of it and wrote it again. Carolyn's fifteen studies had seemed like a mountain of agreement. Now the mountain looked different to him, or the space around it did: every study finding nothing, tucked away where no one could count it.

He did not want to overcorrect. That was the danger he could feel pressing at him, the temptation to decide that the Osaka group was right simply because they were the underdogs of his afternoon. He had no reason to think so. The Rotterdam study was larger; the Osaka one had a cleaner method; both claims could sit in his head at once without either being false. What he could say, honestly, was that fifteen positive results meant less than fifteen seemed to mean, because of what might be unpublished, and that this did not tell him which article was correct, only how much caution the whole comparison deserved.

The barista began stacking chairs on the far side of the room, which was an injunction Olivier chose to interpret as applying to everyone but him. He stayed at the window table and wrote a full paragraph, then a second. In the second paragraph he put the Osaka article first, and gave it the sentence it had earned: that a null result, published despite finding nothing, might be the rarest kind of paper in the field, and that its dullness was exactly why it mattered.

His mother texted twice, then called. He let it ring, packed slowly, folded the articles into his bag with the Osaka one on top, and left money on the table beside the empty saucer. Outside the air had cooled. At the bus stop he read the photograph of Ms. Sok's marginal note once more, then typed to Carolyn, since she was the only one who had read all fifteen: "Did any of them find nothing?" The reply came before the bus did. "One. I didn't use it. It seemed off-message."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Raising the temperature for an exothermic reaction decreases its equilibrium constant, while raising it for an endothermic reaction increases the constant.
story:
The chemistry class had the science museum to itself for two hours on a Tuesday, and Ms. Bautista had given each of them a worksheet with a single question on it: explain how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium. Blake had put his phone in his pocket at nine, taken it out at nine-fifteen, and now Mariah was leaning against the rail beside the equilibrium exhibit, watching him not write anything.

"You've been staring at that tank for ten minutes," she said.

The tank was a sealed column of amber liquid with a valve at the bottom. A plaque beside it gave a data table, equilibrium constants for the reaction inside at three temperatures. Blake copied the numbers onto his worksheet, then read them again to make sure he'd copied them right. At the lower temperature the constant was large. At the higher temperature it was smaller. Every step up the table, the value fell.

"That's backwards," he said. "Hotter should mean more product. That's how everything works. More heat, more happening."

Youcef arrived with a pretzel from the café, which he held out to no one. "That's not chemistry, that's hedonism," he said. "More heat, more fun. Chemistry doesn't care what you want."

Blake ignored him. He'd predicted the opposite in class yesterday, out loud, in front of everyone, and Ms. Bautista had written his answer on the board without correcting it. She did that sometimes, let a wrong idea sit in the room like a chair nobody would claim. He'd walked out still believing it, and now the table said otherwise, and he had forty minutes.

He read the plaque twice more. The reaction was described as exothermic, and the table showed the constant dropping as the temperature rose. He turned to the empty back of his worksheet and wrote it out as two sentences, then crossed out the second one, then wrote it again. If he only had this table, he could still be wrong in general. One reaction wasn't a rule.
