"I need the other exhibit," he said. "The endothermic one, upstairs. The cold tank."

"Youcef and I were going to sit by the pendulum," Mariah said. "There are benches."

"There are benches upstairs."

The upstairs gallery was quieter, and the second exhibit was older, its paint chipped at one corner, but it had a table too. This reaction was labeled endothermic, and here the numbers climbed as the temperature rose. Small constant at low temperature, larger at high. Blake stood in front of it with his worksheet flattened against the glass.

"So it goes both ways," he said. "Exothermic, the constant falls when you heat it. Endothermic, the constant rises. They're mirror images."

"Congratulations," Youcef said from a bench. "You've prognosticated what the plaque already said."

"Shut up. I didn't prognosticate anything. I read two tables and compared them." He sat down on the floor with his back against the exhibit casing, because the bench was taken by Youcef's legs. He wrote out the rule and then, underneath it, wrote what he didn't know: why. The tables told him the direction, both directions, but nothing about the cause, and he wasn't sure he could defend the rule if someone asked him why it held. He circled the word why and left it circled.

Mariah came over and looked at his page. "So what was your answer in class yesterday?"

"The opposite. I said heating pushes everything toward products no matter what."

"Ms. Bautista is downstairs."

"I know."

He found her near the pendulum, explaining Foucault to a parent who had tagged along with a younger sibling. Blake waited until she finished, then held out the worksheet. She read it without expression, which was usual, and handed it back.

"Where did the why come from?" she said.

"The tables don't say. I marked it because I can't answer it."

She almost smiled. "It stays marked for now. The direction you can defend. Read the table at the tank again before we leave, the cold setting, and tell me what you expect."

He went down ahead of the group. The tank had a cooling coil, and a docent, a taciturn old man in a gray jacket, turned the valve when Blake asked. The liquid in the column deepened toward orange as it chilled. Exothermic reaction, lower temperature, and Blake watched the color and thought: larger constant, more product, the shift running the way he'd said it wouldn't yesterday. He'd had it exactly backward until two tables on the second floor corrected him.

He wrote his final prediction on the worksheet and handed it to Ms. Bautista at the bus, and she read it and put it in her folder and said, "Full marks."

Youcef clapped him on the shoulder. "So what does the smart money say the grade on yesterday's board answer was?"

"Zero. She never graded the board."

"Then you got full marks today for fixing a wrong answer nobody ever counted," Youcef said, and bit into the pretzel he'd been carrying since ten.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The Haymarket affair in Chicago on May 4, 1886, grew out of protests for an eight-hour workday and is considered the origin of May 1 as International Workers' Day.
story:
Nicole clocked in at 4:58 and found the break room papered with a single photocopied sheet. SCHEDULE CHANGE, it said, in the manager's habitually irascible capitals. All Sunday shifts extended to nine hours, effective immediately, no overtime rate because the extra hours fell under forty for the week. Beneath it someone had written "again" in pencil, and beneath that, in different handwriting, "check the law."

She folded a copy into her apron pocket and carried it out to the register, where Theodore was bagging expired pastries for the donation bin. "Did you see this?" she asked. He had seen it. He had also done the arithmetic: on Sundays the bakery ran with three people instead of six, so nine hours meant nine hours on your feet with no second break, because the second break only kicked in past a threshold the schedule was built to duck. "They know exactly where the line is," he said. "They stand on the safe side of it and lean."

Nicole wanted the money for September. Textbooks, a bus pass, the deposit on a room she had not yet seen. Nine hours at straight time was not nothing, and refusing it felt like a luxury she was computing against her own future. But at home that night her mother, who folded hospital laundry for a living, said only, "We have a union for a reason," and went back to her crossword, as if that settled something Nicole did not yet understand. It destabilized her more than an argument would have, because it assumed she already knew.

At school the next morning she found Arnav in the library and asked him, straight out, why workers marched on the first of May. He was the person for this; his grandfather had organized textile mills in another country and Arnav treated labour history the way other people treated football. "That's May Day," he said. "International Workers' Day. It goes back to the Haymarket affair in Chicago, May 4, 1886. It grew out of protests for an eight-hour workday." He showed her the page in his book, a woodcut of a crowd and a wagon. "That's why May 1 is Workers' Day in so many countries. Workers in Chicago got shot at and hanged for asking for eight hours, and the rest of the world remembered it on the first of May."

Nicole read the page twice. Eight hours. She worked nine on Sundays now, at eighteen, a hundred and thirty years later, and it was legal, and nobody was hanged, and the schedule was engineered so precisely around the law that she could not tell whether the law protected her or merely described the shape of what could be done to her. She kept that to herself. Arnav was already onto the next thing, which was a flyer on the library table: a meeting, Thursday, at the community hall, for food service workers in the district. "Some of the coffee shop people are going," he said. "They're trying to sign enough cards to force a vote. A union has to be certified before you can bargain, and bargaining is the only thing that changes a schedule like yours."

"That's collective bargaining," Arnav said, when she asked what the flyer meant by it. "You elect reps, they negotiate wages and hours for everyone, and it's binding. One worker asking for a break is a pest. All of us asking is a position." Nicole thought of the pencil word in the break room, "again," and understood that someone at the bakery had already been thinking this, quietly, without a flyer.

She went to the Thursday meeting. Ms. Gagnon was there, which surprised her until she remembered that Ms. Gagnon taught phys ed and worked summers at the arena canteen; she sat in the second row with her arms folded, listening the way she coached, alert and unhurried. The speaker, a young organizer from the coffee shop campaign, did not speechify. She passed around a sample agreement and pointed to the clauses about scheduling notice and penalty rates, and when a boy from a pizza place asked whether joining would get them all fired, she answered plainly: the labour board covered organizing activity, retaliation was illegal, and illegal was not the same as impossible, so they would document everything, dates and names, from the first day. The room got quieter at that, not louder. Nicole signed a card and wrote her name in full, the way you do on documents that matter.

Signing took ten seconds. What followed took six weeks of small, careful acts: keeping the photocopied schedule in a folder, noting the nights the assistant manager cut breaks at six and a half hours, passing the folder to Theodore, who passed it to the coffee shop workers, whose organizer filed it. When the bakery's manager called Nicole into the office and asked, too casually, who had been talking to the union, she said she had nothing to add, and felt her pulse in her throat the whole time, and did not add it.

The vote passed by one. One card, one signature, possibly hers, possibly the dishwasher's, possibly the woman who frosted cakes and had written "again" in pencil. A first contract would take months to negotiate; the Sunday hours might not change until she was already gone, sitting in a lecture hall in another city, spending money earned under the old rules. That was the part she could not resolve, and she was honest with herself about it: she had acted for people she would never meet, on a timeline she would not benefit from, and she could not prove it had been the rational choice. On her last shift before leaving for college she taped a photocopy of the woodcut, the crowd and the wagon, Chicago 1886, inside her locker door.

"Eight hours," Theodore said behind her, reading it over her shoulder. "And they were asking for the world."

"Just the day, divided fair," Nicole said, and closed the locker.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: Trade based on comparative advantage raises a country's total income, but individual workers in industries that now face cheaper imports can still lose their jobs or wages.
story:
Robert had been assigned the essay on Monday, due Friday, and by Saturday morning he still had nothing but a title and a paragraph so prolix his own eyes slid off it. So he took the bus to the farmers' market with his notebook, on the theory that economics was about people buying and selling, and there would be people buying and selling here.

The market ran three blocks of white tents, and the first thing he noticed was the smell: kettle corn, wet lettuce, cut peaches. Ms. Moretti from his school had a stall near the middle, stacked with jars of her honey, and she waved him over before he had decided whether to be seen.

"Robert. Buy something or help me carry these crates, your choice."

He helped her carry the crates. She was smaller than he was and the crates were heavier than they looked, and she gave him a bruised apple for his trouble, which he ate walking. Somewhere between the flower stall and the bread stand, an older man at a folding table caught his attention, mostly because the man was not selling anything. He sat behind a sign that read HONEY, MS. MORETTI'S, SAME PRICE, and he was reading a folded newspaper with a pen.

"You're with Moretti," the man said, not looking up. "You carried her crates. I'm her brother, I sit here so she can work the crowd."

Robert said he was doing an economics essay, and the man grunted in a way that meant something. On the table beside the newspaper was a thermos and a union pin, scuffed gold, pinned to a canvas hat.

"What's the essay on?"

"Trade. Comparative advantage. It's this idea that even if one country is better at making everything, both countries still gain from trading, because each one makes the thing it's relatively best at." Robert had practiced the sentence in the mirror, which was probably why it came out sounding practiced.

The man set down his pen. "I worked thirty-one years at a plant off Route 9. They closed it. Stuff comes in cheaper from somewhere else now."

Robert felt the apple go dry in his mouth. He wanted to say something about efficiency, about totals, and he could hear how it would sound.

"Here's what I never got," the man said. "My nephew, he's your age, tells me the country's richer because of the trade. And I say, fine, the country. But the country didn't clock in at that plant. I did. Two hundred and some of us did."

"Ms. Moretti?" Robert called, because he did not know what else to do, and she came over wiping her hands on her apron.

"Robert, this is my brother."

"I gathered," she said. She put a hand briefly on her brother's shoulder and then went back to a customer, and Robert understood that she had done that on purpose, given him a moment he could take or not take.

He sat down on the empty camp stool beside the table. He did not cogitate out loud, which his mother always teased him about; he thought hard and quietly, turning the man's sentence over. The country's richer. The country. He pulled out his notebook and wrote it plainly this time: trade based on comparative advantage raises a country's total income. Then he sat looking at it, because the second half would not come, and the second half was sitting next to him.

"So who got the gain?" the man asked. It was not hostile. It was a real question, one he had maybe asked the newspaper a hundred times.

"Everybody and nobody," Robert said slowly. "The total goes up. But the people who made the thing that now comes in cheaper, they can lose their jobs or their wages. Both things are true at once. That's actually the part nobody writes down."

"Both things at once," the man repeated. He looked at the pin on his hat, then out at the crowd, at a woman buying four jars of honey, at a kid dropping a peach and picking it up again. "That's the first thing anybody's said to me about it that didn't sound like it was written on a pamphlet."

Robert wrote the second half of the sentence. He did not write a conclusion, because he could not find one that was honest. He wrote instead: maybe the essay is about why the gains get counted more often than the losses. He thought about telling the man that the plant closing might have had other causes, and then he didn't, because he didn't know, and pretending to know would be the pamphlet again. There was no grand design to any of it, no teleology where the loss turned out to be for the best, and he was tired of people who needed one.

A customer came to the table and the man sold her a jar, made change from a tin, thanked her by name. Robert watched him do it well, easily, a man good at something.

"You'll write it, then," the man said.

"I'll write it," Robert said. "Can I come back and read you the part about the plant? I won't use your name."

The man considered, and behind them Ms. Moretti called out that the kettle corn man was giving away the burnt batches at noon, and did anybody want some. Her brother smiled for the first time all morning.

"Bring the corn," he said, "and read slow."

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Under US law, an artwork is protected by copyright automatically the moment it is created in a fixed form; registration is voluntary, though needed before suing over a US work.
story:
The attic of her grandmother's house smelled of cedar and old paper, and Camille had claimed it for the summer because the north-facing window gave a light that flattened nothing. She had eleven weeks before her college portfolio was due, and the requirement she kept circling was the strange one: ten artworks bound to a single theme, plus a statement, one page, explaining what the work was doing. She had painted since she was nine, but she had never once had to say what the painting was for.

Her theme had arrived almost by accident. On the second weekend she found her grandmother's box of photographs from a town in northern Manitoba, grain silos and black spruce and a lake the colour of pewter, and she understood that what she wanted to paint was the boreal edge of things, the line where forest thinned into muskeg and sky took over. She painted the silos first, then the spruce, then her grandmother's hands holding a photograph of the lake. The paintings came easier than the statement. Every draft she wrote sounded like a museum label written by someone pretending to be her.

Marissa came up on a Thursday with a bag of cherries and her laptop, and sprawled on the attic floor beside the drying racks. She was applying to the same programs, and where Camille had gone quiet and deliberate, Marissa had gone strategic, spreadsheets of deadlines, a folder of reference artists. When Camille showed her the three finished pieces, Marissa photographed them immediately.

"You have to post these," she said. "Half of admissions is them finding you before you find them. Everyone builds a feed over the summer."

"I don't know," Camille said. "If I put them online, doesn't that mean anyone can just use them? Take them, print them, whatever?"

Marissa pulled a pit from between her teeth and considered the paintings. "That's why people watermark. Or don't post at all until after decisions."

That night Camille couldn't sleep, and she went down to the kitchen where her grandmother was dozing over a crossword, and asked her, straight out, whether she had ever worried about that, about making things and then losing them. Her grandmother had painted for thirty years, church basements, community halls, gifts. "Copyright," her grandmother said, tapping the crossword. "I think that's an eight-letter word for what you're worried about." She didn't know anything beyond the word, and she went to bed.

So Camille looked it up herself, on the slow computer in the front room, taking notes on the back of a grocery receipt. What she found stopped her. Under US law, an artwork was protected by copyright automatically, the moment it was created in a fixed form. The painting on the rack upstairs already belonged to her in the eyes of the law, the way the attic window belonged to the house. Registration was voluntary, she read, though it was needed before suing over a US work. She read the sentence twice, then a third time, because the two halves seemed to disagree. Protected automatically, and yet not fully, not without a further step she could choose to take or not take.

She sat with the receipt in her hand and thought about her grandmother, who had made things for thirty years and given nearly all of them away, and about Marissa, who wanted everything branded and defended before it touched the internet. Those had seemed like opposite positions, but the law she had just read suggested something else, something she could almost hold. Making a thing fixed it as hers; posting it did not abrogate that. Sharing was not surrender. And still the voluntary part lingered, the gap between automatic protection and the standing to sue, which meant the certainty was real but not total, and she would have to decide what that gap was worth to her. She wrote in her sketchbook, "protected when made. voluntary to register. needed to sue." Then, underneath, in smaller letters, "so the fear was half wrong."

The next morning Marissa came by again, and Camille read her the grocery receipt on the porch steps, word for word, and watched her friend's shoulders drop an inch. "So I don't have to watermark everything like a paranoid person," Marissa said. "It's mine the second I make it." Camille said yes, hers the second she made it, and then they sat quiet, splitting the last of the cherries, spitting the pits over the rail into the garden.

She finished the tenth painting in August, the lake in pewter light, and the statement the night after, one page, mostly true. She photographed the portfolio in the attic with the boreal light coming full across it, and then, before she could revise anything further, she uploaded the files to the application portal, pressed submit, and closed the laptop on the sound of her grandmother coming up the stairs with tea.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Binary search works only on sorted data: it compares the target with the middle item and throws away the half of the list that cannot contain it.
story:
The study room smelled of dry-erase marker and someone's leftover instant noodles, and Sara had promised herself she would not leave until the club's roster problem was solved. Cullen had written the search himself, forty lines of Java, and for two weeks it had been reporting that members were missing when they were plainly on the list. Elianna kept saying it worked on her laptop. Ms. McKenzie, the librarian who had let the coding club claim the room on Thursday nights, poked her head in around six and asked only whether they were keeping the noise down.

"Watch," Cullen said, turning the screen toward Sara. He typed a name, Okafor, and hit enter. "Not found." He scrolled the roster file, and there it was, Okafor, fourth from the top, no typo, no stray space. "See? It's haunted."

Sara had spent the summer shelving returns at this same library, and something about the situation itched at her. She pulled the chair closer and asked him to walk her through the algorithm instead of the output. He was taciturn when he code-reviewed, answering in fragments, but he pointed at a block that found the middle of the list, compared the target against it, and then cut the list in half, keeping only the side where the answer could still be.

Something surfaced, a memory from before the club, before she'd known the word algorithm. Her grandfather's dictionary, the enormous one on the stand in his hallway, and the game he played with her when she was nine: open to the middle, he'd say, and if your word comes before this page, ignore the whole back of the book. She'd loved the feeling of it, the way the dictionary shrank in her hands, hundreds of pages discarded at a time, until the word was trapped on a single page. He'd never called it anything. He'd just tap the paper and say, "Half, then half again."

She said, "That only works because the dictionary's alphabetized."

Cullen frowned. Elianna leaned over from the far side of the table, where she'd been quietly copy-pasting test data. "So?" Cullen said.

"So look at your roster." Sara scrolled to the top of the file. The names weren't alphabetical, weren't in any order she could see; they were in the order people had joined the club, which meant Patel came before Alvarez because Patel had signed up first at the activities fair. The code was comparing Okafor against the middle of the list and throwing away the half of the list that couldn't contain him, except that with an unordered list, either half could contain him. It wasn't haunted. It was doing exactly what Cullen had asked, and what he'd asked was wrong.

Elianna's tests had passed, it turned out, because she'd generated her test data sorted, out of habit, and had never once used the real roster. The twist that made Sara laugh out loud, though, came a minute later: when Cullen sorted the roster file and reran the search, it found Okafor instantly, and it also found three members they had all believed had quit, names the old linear search, the one that trudged from the first entry to the last, had somehow never surfaced. "It wasn't losing people," Sara said slowly. "It was hiding the fact that we'd been losing people. Two different bugs stacked on each other."

"I hate that," Cullen said, with feeling.

"Which one?"

"Both. The second one more."

They stayed until the lights dimmed for closing. Cullen rewrote the search so it checked the data first, and Elianna built a test with names deliberately shuffled. Ms. McKenzie came through at nine collecting abandoned coffee cups, and when Elianna tried to contextualize the evening for her, explaining how a faster method carried a hidden price, that it demanded the world be arranged before it could promise anything, Ms. McKenzie only nodded and said, "That's also true of card catalogs," and left them with the cups.

Walking out through the lobby, past the returns cart she still knew by heart, Sara tried to say what she'd concluded, and found she couldn't make it tidy. She liked the linear search, in a way. It was honest, a bromide in code: check everything, miss nothing, however long it takes. And she liked the binary search, its halving confidence, the memory of her grandfather's hand over hers. The position she settled on, if it was a position, was that neither one was a virtue by itself; the fast way worked only where somebody had already done the slow, careful work of putting things in order, and forgetting that order was itself a thing someone had made was how you ended up telling members they didn't exist. What stayed uncertain was how you'd ever know, in advance, which kind of problem you were holding.

At the door, Cullen zipped his laptop into its bag. "Next semester I'm sorting the roster the day people sign up," he said.

"Good," said Sara.

"And you're explaining it to the new members. The middle thing. You made it make sense."

She pushed the library door open with her shoulder, into the cold. "Fine. But I'm bringing a dictionary."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Sorting a list takes more work than one linear search, so sorting just to run binary search pays off only when the same data will be searched many times.
story:
The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and burnt coffee, and the folding tables trembled every time a team dragged a toolbox across them. Jonathan knelt behind their robot with a multimeter, listening to Abbas argue with Sana about the code.

"The sensor gives us part numbers in whatever order they arrive," Sana said, tapping her laptop. "We have to find the one that matches the target on the field. Abbas wants to sort the whole list first and run binary search. He read about it last night."

"Binary search is beautiful," Abbas said. "You look at the middle, throw away half, look at the new middle, throw away half again. On a sorted list it beats checking every entry one by one. A linear search, I mean, checking each item in turn, that's the slow way."

Jonathan tested the last connection and sat back on his heels. "How many times do we search the list?"

Abbas blinked at him. "Once. The robot reads the target once and finds the matching part."

"Then why sort?" Jonathan asked. He wasn't trying to be clever; he genuinely wanted to know, because somewhere between the multimeter and the question, two pictures had collided in his head. He'd spent the morning thinking like Abbas, dazzled by the elegant method, and the afternoon thinking like a builder, counting every millisecond before the buzzer. "Sorting the list takes more work than one linear search. If we only search once, we'd be paying all that work for nothing."

Sana stopped typing. Abbas opened his mouth, closed it, and pulled his notebook toward him, scrawling arrows and crossing them out. "So the sort only pays off," he said slowly, "if we're going to search the same data many times."

"Right. Like a parts catalogue you query all season. Not a one-time lookup." Jonathan felt something invigorate in him, a clean surge of certainty, and it felt dangerous, because he'd been wrong twice already that morning and both times he'd felt exactly this.

Ms. Li, their coach, drifted past with a clipboard and heard the last exchange. She didn't correct anyone. She only said, "Eleven minutes to inspection," and moved on, which Jonathan understood to mean the decision belonged to them.

Sana deleted the sort function and wrote the loop that walked the list item by item. Her fingers moved fast, and the fan on the laptop whirred against the smell of another team's soldering iron two tables over. The robot's arm clicked through its test cycle. Abbas kept rubbing the back of his neck, and finally he said, "I stayed up until two learning binary search."

"I know," Jonathan said. "It wasn't wasted. We'll use it at regionals, where the same catalogue gets searched over and over."

"That's not the same as it being used today."

"No. It isn't."

They passed inspection with four minutes left. In the first match, the robot read the target, walked the unsorted list, and found the matching part in under a second, faster than the team beside them, whose sort routine had eaten their entire window and left their robot motionless at the starting square. Abbas watched them and said nothing, which was somehow worse than gloating.

They lost the round anyway, on a mechanical failure no algorithm could touch: a stripped gear in the shoulder joint, the arm sagging at a tectonic angle, the whole structure leaning like something after an earthquake. Sana sat down on the floor with her back against the table and laughed until she sounded like she was crying, and then she was crying a little, and Jonathan sat down beside her.

Afterward, while the volunteers swept and the scoreboard glowed with other teams' names, Abbas offered Jonathan the last granola bar, half a bar really, the other half already eaten on principle. "Restitution," he said. "For making us argue about sorting for twenty minutes."

"That was a good argument," Jonathan said. He took the bar anyway.

He was still turning the thing over as they packed up. The linear search had been right today; the binary search would be right next month; and he couldn't shake the suspicion that the difference between right and wrong had less to do with the code than with what a person knew in advance about the future, which was nothing. He didn't say that out loud. He coiled the cables, and Sana zipped the toolbox, and Abbas shouldered the robot crate like it was heavier than it was.

"Same bus?" Abbas asked.

"Same bus," Jonathan said, and picked up the multimeter.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Subtext is the meaning beneath what characters actually say, such as anger or love that a line never names out loud.
story:
Mr. Lau had moved the desks against the wall of the black box theatre, which meant, everyone understood, that this was not a class where you got to sit down. "You have four weeks," he said, "to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from your own life. Not a symbol of a moment. The moment." He said the word sedimentary the way other teachers said pop quiz, complaining that most teenage writing arrived in layers, excuse on top of excuse on top of what actually happened, and that he wanted them to drill down to the rock. Then he handed out index cards and told them to write the worst thing they were willing to admit in this room.

Jeremy wrote about the night his father came home late from the hospital where his mother was, and Jeremy, who had been awake and frightened for hours, said only, "There's leftover pasta." His father said, "I ate." That was the entire conversation. He passed the card forward face down, as if that hid anything.

Grayden, who sat behind him, had written about his brother and read it aloud without being asked, which was Grayden's way. "So in mine, the brother character says, 'I'm angry because Dad always liked you better,' and the other one says, 'I'm sad too,' and then they hug it out." He looked pleased. Mr. Lau looked like a man watching a plane taxi toward a cliff.

"It's very clear," Mr. Lau said, in the tone he used when clarity was the problem. He asked the class whether anyone had noticed anything about the cards, and Everett, who wanted to be a lawyer and argued like it, said that everyone had apparently decided to have extremely articulate breakdowns, stating every feeling with footnotes. Grayden said that at least his was honest, and Everett said that nobody in real life was honest on schedule.

Jeremy had been quiet, because he was doing the arithmetic. If the pasta line and the "I ate" line were the whole conversation, then the actual conversation had happened somewhere else, underneath, and neither of them had named it out loud, which was, he realized, the entire architecture of that night. He raised his hand, which he did maybe once a semester. "It's like subtext," he said. "Subtext is the meaning beneath what characters actually say, such as anger or love that a line never names out loud." He heard his own voice do it and immediately wanted the sentence back, because it came out sounding like a textbook, and also because he had just accidentally explained his card to twenty-six people.

Mr. Lau did not rescue him. "So your play would be two people talking about pasta."

"Ten minutes of pasta," Jeremy said.

"Write it," said Mr. Lau, and moved on to a girl whose card, glimpsed upside down, appeared to involve a locker and an apology never delivered.

For the rest of the period they workshopped in trios, and Jeremy ended up with Grayden and Everett, which was less a grouping than a weather system. Everett opened by trying to problematize the whole assignment, arguing that a room where everyone had to confess was less a drama class than a small oligarchy of one teacher deciding whose pain counted as literature. Mr. Lau, passing behind him, said, "Fine, stage that instead," and kept walking, and Everett shut up, which Jeremy found educational.

Grayden, though, had gone quiet and was rereading his card. "The hug it out thing," he said finally. "My brother didn't say any of that. He took the car without asking and I didn't say anything, I just let the air out of the tires, and then we stood in the driveway not talking for like an hour." He looked up. "That's the real one. I made the other version because the real one's boring."

"It's not boring," Jeremy said. "It's the most interesting thing you've said all year, and you once lectured us for forty minutes about fantasy football." He told them about the pasta, since the card had already outed it, and about how his draft had opened with the father character explaining he was scared, in case the audience was, apparently, from another planet. Grayden said that maybe they should write a scene where nobody said one true thing and the audience had to catch it on the bounce, and Everett, recovering, said the prosecution could live with that.

They spent the last ten minutes on the floor of the hallway outside the theatre, where Mr. Lau had banished the noise, blocking a driveway scene with two chairs standing in for the car. Grayden played his own brother and kept almost saying the apology, catching it each time and replacing it with "You checking the tires?" and "Some of them were low," and it was funny and then, somewhere around the fourth repetition, it stopped being funny and neither of them looked at the other, and Everett, watching with his arms folded like a judge, said quietly, "Okay. That works. I hate that it works."

Mr. Lau leaned out of the theatre door. "Whatever is happening out here, do exactly that on Friday." The bell rang over him, unhelpfully, as bells do.

Jeremy walked to his next class with the index card in his pocket, and on the back of it, in pencil, he wrote "leftover pasta / I ate," and underneath, nothing yet, and drew a line for where the rest would go.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Encapsulation means hiding a class's data behind methods, so other code can use the object without depending on how it stores its data.
story:
The projector in the camp's west lab had a dead pixel that Lucas kept mistaking for a period at the end of his code. By Wednesday afternoon he was squinting at it, chin on his fist, while his BankAccount class sat on the screen with its balance field hanging out in the open, public and unguarded, like a wallet left on a bench. The Friday showcase was two days away. Ms. Yip had promised the winning pair a tour of the actual server room, the cold one in the basement with the cables, and Lucas wanted that more than he wanted to admit out loud.

"You're doing it wrong," Elie said, dropping into the chair beside him without being invited. Elie had a way of stating things as verdicts, the way a referee does, and Lucas had learned by the second day of camp not to litigate every call. He picked his arguments now, mostly.

"It compiles."

"Compiling isn't the same as not being wrong."

Meagan leaned across the table, hair tied up with a pencil, and pointed at Lucas's screen. "I'm using your class for the demo, remember? My ledger pulls the balance straight off your object. If you touch anything, I touch everything."

"So don't touch anything," Lucas said, and he meant it, and that was the whole problem, though he didn't know it yet.

That night the lab stayed open until ten. Lucas stayed until ten, then later than he should have, sneaking back after lights-out along the gravel path past the canoe rack, because he had decided the balance should hold cents as well as dollars. It was a small change. He changed the field from an int to a double, went to bed pleased with himself, and slept badly in the hot cabin with the truculent fan clicking through its rotation.

Thursday morning, Meagan's screen was red. Forty errors, cascading down the compiler output like something knocked over. She didn't yell. She sat very still with her hands off the keyboard, which was worse, and said, "Lucas," in the flat voice people use when they're deciding whether to be angry or just tired. Her code had reached into his object and grabbed the field directly, and when the field changed its type, everything she'd built on it stopped fitting. She had trusted his storage, and he'd broken the trust without knowing he'd made any.

Elie, meanwhile, ran his own demo flawlessly. That was the part Lucas couldn't understand, and it bothered him through lunch, through the afternoon session, through the pickup game nobody really played hard at. Elie's account class did the same thing Meagan's ledger needed, pulled the same values, printed the same receipt. Lucas had watched him type it. So how was Elie green while Meagan was red?

He found out by accident, which is how he found out most things. Elie left his laptop unlocked during the swim block, and Lucas, meaning only to borrow the fan cable, saw the commit history. At 11:52 the previous night, Elie had changed his own balance field from an int to a double. The exact change Lucas had made. And nothing in Elie's project had broken, not one line, because Elie's fields were private and his getters were the only door in. The other code used his object without depending on how it stored its data.

"It's called encapsulation," Elie said later, when Lucas cornered him by the canteen, still dripping, towel around his neck. "Hiding the data behind methods." He said it the way you'd say the name of a band you assumed everyone had heard of, and Lucas could have called him an egoist for it, and didn't, because the demonstration had already done all the arguing.

That evening Lucas rebuilt his class field by field, private now, a getter for the balance, another for the owner's name, a test in a separate file that created an account, deposited forty dollars, and demanded the number back. Meagan sat beside him and rewired her ledger to call the methods instead of reaching into the field, and when Lucas changed the balance to a double again, deliberately, to prove it, her screen stayed green. She exhaled through her nose, almost a laugh.

At the showcase on Friday they didn't win. A pair from the east cabin did something with a weather station and a paper cup, and the judges liked the paper cup. Ms. Yip came by their table afterward, looked at the two screens side by side, the private fields and the passing tests, and said only, "Run it again." Lucas ran it again.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Montana is the one US state where, after a probationary period, an employer generally needs good cause to fire a worker, under its 1987 Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act.
story:
The restaurant sat at the edge of the highway where the road to Billings began its long climb, and Sierra had walked past it every school day for three years without once going in. Now she stood at the door in her only blouse, a résumé her mother had helped her format folded twice in her back pocket, watching a waitress balance four plates up one forearm. When Mr. Grant came out from behind the register, he looked her over once and asked if she could start Saturday.

She had not expected it to be that fast. At home she had rehearsed answers to questions about her weaknesses and her five-year plans, and instead the whole interview had lasted ninety seconds, circumscribed by his obvious need for someone, anyone, who would show up on weekends. She said yes before she had fully decided, and then walked the four blocks home in a kind of daze, the smell of fryer grease still on her sleeves.

That night Zachary came over with his laptop, ostensibly to study for the chemistry final, actually to sprawl on her floor and argue. His cousin in Montana had texted him something that had gotten under his skin. "She got written up at her waitressing job," he said, "and her manager told her the write-up means she can be fired for any reason now. She's freaking out. But my dad says bosses can fire whoever they want, whenever. That's just how it works."

Sierra had believed the same thing an hour ago. It had the flat certainty of something everyone repeats until it becomes furniture, an assumption so ordinary nobody looks under it. But something about the cousin's situation bothered her, the idea of a seventeen-year-old girl two states over being frightened by a threat that might not even be real. She took the laptop out of Zachary's hands and started typing.

What she found surprised both of them. Their state was like most; the cousin's was not. "Montana," she read aloud, then read it again to be sure. "It's the one state where, after a probationary period, an employer generally needs good cause to fire a worker." Zachary sat up. She scrolled further and found the name of the law, the Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act, passed in 1987. "So she's still on probation?" Zachary asked, and Sierra said she'd have to ask, because the page didn't say how long probation ran and she wasn't going to guess at something that mattered. She typed a message to the cousin through Zachary's phone: not you're safe, not relax, just check your hire date against your probation period, and here's the law's name.

Zachary argued the other side anyway, because that was what Zachary did, loudly and with his whole body, so that Sierra's mother eventually knocked on the door and called him obstreperous, which made him briefly proud. His position was that a rule on paper wouldn't help a girl whose manager already disliked her, that a boss who wanted you gone would find a way, cause or no cause. Sierra didn't disagree. She had learned enough in one restaurant interview to know that power doesn't disappear because a statute circumscribes it. But she kept thinking about the difference between a threat that is legal and a threat that only sounds legal, and about how the cousin had no way of knowing which one she'd received until someone looked it up. Knowing the rule didn't fix everything. Not knowing it fixed nothing.

On Saturday she bused tables for six hours, and by hour four her arms ached and a cook had yelled at her for stacking plates wrong, and she understood that a job like this was mostly endurance, the kind of work that draws on some deep patience the way a well draws on an aquifer, unseen reserves you never knew you had until the pump started running. She scraped food into the compost and wiped ketchup off a booster seat and did not quit.

Near closing, Mr. Grant stopped her by the register. He mentioned, almost as an aside, that her first month was a trial period, and that after that she'd be on regular staff, the way he said it implying she should feel grateful for the softening. Sierra thought of the cousin in Montana, and of Zachary's father's flat certainty, and of the paragraph she had read twice because she didn't trust herself to get it right the first time. She took off her apron and folded it over her arm.

"Do I need to sign anything for the trial part?" she asked.

Mr. Grant looked at her for a moment, then pulled a form from under the register and slid it toward her, tapping the line where her name would go.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Negative space is the empty area around and between the subjects of an image, and artists often draw that space to get a shape's outline right.
story:
The kitchen chair had defeated Florence for forty minutes, which was long enough that she had begun to take it personally. She sat at the kitchen table with her sketchbook propped against the sugar bowl, a pencil worn down to a stub, and a drawing of a chair that looked like a chair drawn by someone who had heard about chairs secondhand. The seat tilted upward at an angle no carpenter would permit. The legs splayed like a startled animal. She erased the back left leg for the third time and the paper began to pill.

"You're grinding your teeth," said Emilie, who was across the table supposedly working on a chemistry lab but mostly watching Florence suffer. "Also you just said a bad word at a chair."

"I said it at the drawing. The chair is innocent." Florence turned the sketchbook around. "See? Ms. Fischer wants a chair for the portfolio thing. A whole chair, accurate, by Friday. And I can draw faces, Emilie. I can draw hands, which everybody says are impossible. But this chair looks like it's melting."

Emilie leaned over, chewing her pen in a way Florence had asked her not to. "It does kind of look like it's melting. It's a Dali chair."

"That's not comforting."

Kailyn arrived at the half hour mark, as she always did, carrying her own homework and no intention of doing it. She dropped into the third chair, the one Florence wasn't drawing, and looked at the wreckage. "Ooh," she said, which was her standard opening for someone else's disaster. "Why is it leaning?"

"It's not leaning. I mean, the real one isn't leaning. That's the problem. When I look at the chair I can see it's fine, and then I draw it and it's wrong, and I can't find where the wrongness starts." Florence flipped to a fresh page, then flipped back, then flipped forward again, as though the correct chair might be hiding on a sheet she hadn't tried.

Kailyn, who was enthralling herself with the biscuit tin, offered a view over the lid. "Maybe you should draw something easier. Draw a biscuit. Draw the tin."

"Ms. Fischer specifically said chair. She said, and I quote, 'If you can draw a chair, you can draw anything, because a chair will lie to you.'" Florence paused. "I didn't understand that at the time. I understand it even less now."

Emilie had gone quiet, which for Emilie meant she was either thinking or asleep with her eyes open. "My gran does watercolors," she said slowly. "Rivers and things, all that riparian stuff, banks and reeds. She says the water is the hardest part because it's really just the shape of everything around it. The gap between the reeds, the space under the bridge." She frowned at her own sentence. "I might be saying that wrong."

Florence's pencil stopped in the air. Something turned over in her head, the way a key turns before you're sure it's the right key. She looked at the chair. Then she looked, deliberately, at what was not the chair: the triangle of kitchen wall between the legs, the window framed by the backrest, the bright rectangles of floor showing through the rungs. She had spent forty minutes drawing the wooden parts and failing. She had not once drawn the air.

"Okay," she said. "Okay okay okay. Don't talk to me."

"You love when we talk to you," said Kailyn, but Florence was already sketching, fast, the triangle under the seat, the wedge between the second and third rung, the notches of doorway visible around the chair's silhouette. She drew the empties and let the solid parts happen as the leftover edges between them, and the chair assembled itself out of everything it wasn't. When she held the page at arm's length, the legs were legs. The seat lay flat, horizontal, truthful.

"How," said Emilie, flatly.

"It's called negative space," Florence said, mostly to the page. "The empty area around and between the subject. Ms. Fischer mentioned it like once, months ago, and I thought it was just an art-class phrase. But you can draw the gaps instead of the thing, and the outline comes out right." She turned the sketchbook so they could both see. "Emilie's gran was basically saying the same thing about the river. Which means either I've discovered something everyone knows, or everyone knows something I just discovered."

"That's an epistemology problem," said Kailyn, with her mouth full of biscuit. "Whether a thing counts as discovered if other people already had it. I learned that word this week and I've been waiting for a chance."

"You've been waiting two days."

"It was a long wait."

Florence started the drawing again on good paper, the heavy stock she'd been saving, and this time she began with the window behind the chair, with the triangles and the door-shaped holes, letting the chair arrive as the outline of its own absence. It felt, she thought, a little like the arguments she and Emilie had been having all year about whether people should be judged by intentions or effects, except that here she didn't have to choose. She could hold the object and the emptiness in the same page and let each one correct the other. What she still couldn't tell was whether the good drawing was luck, and she wouldn't know until she drew a second chair, and she wasn't going to think about the second chair yet.

The back door opened and her mother came in with shopping bags, looked at the table, at three girls, at two packets of homework entirely untouched, and said nothing, which was worse than saying something. Florence bent her head and kept her pencil moving along the edge of a gap between the second and third rung, and behind her the kettle clicked on.
